query.original_query: sparse autoencoder features detect hallucination invalid generation early stopping generative model

sub_queries.semantic_query: sparse autoencoder features detect hallucination invalid generation early stopping generative model LLM interpretability
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate whether sparse autoencoder (SAE) features learned from the residual stream of a generative language model can serve as early indicators of hallucination during autoregressive generation. Using a dictionary learning approach, we extract monosemantic features from the model’s intermediate layers and analyze their activation patterns across both factual and hallucinated outputs. Our analysis reveals that certain features consistently activate prior to the generation of invalid or factually inconsistent tokens, often preceding the onset of hallucination by several steps. We find that these features correspond to latent concepts related to uncertainty, entity mismatch, and factual recall, and that their activation magnitude correlates with downstream generation fidelity. By monitoring feature-level dynamics during inference, we demonstrate that SAE-based representations can detect hallucination onset before the model commits to an erroneous continuation. Results show that feature steering or early stopping based on these signals reduces hallucination rates without requiring external knowledge bases or retraining. Our findings suggest that SAE features provide a mechanistic window into the model’s internal state, enabling interpretable and intervention-based hallucination detection in generative language models.

sub_queries.semantic_query: sparse autoencoder features detect hallucination invalid generation early stopping generative model
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate whether features extracted from sparse autoencoders (SAEs) applied to the internal activations of a generative language model can serve as early indicators of hallucination or invalid generation. Using a trained SAE on a transformer-based model, we measured feature activation patterns during autoregressive decoding on a dataset of factual and counterfactual prompts. We hypothesized that specific SAE features, corresponding to latent concepts such as factual consistency or entity plausibility, would exhibit distinct activation trajectories prior to the onset of an invalid output. Results indicate that the magnitude and rate of change of certain feature activations diverge significantly between valid and hallucinated generations, often preceding the generation of the first erroneous token. Findings support the hypothesis that SAE-derived features provide a signal for early stopping, enabling the truncation of generation before the model commits to a false statement. This approach offers a mechanistic, interpretable alternative to post-hoc detection methods, leveraging the model’s own learned representations without requiring external knowledge bases.

papers.title: Unsupervised Real-Time Hallucination Detection based on the Internal States of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can hallucinations in large language models be detected in real-time using the models' internal states, without requiring manual annotations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MIND, an unsupervised framework for real-time hallucination detection using the internal states of LLMs, and HELM, a new benchmark for evaluating hallucination detection across multiple LLMs.
papers.conclusion: MIND is an effective unsupervised method for real-time hallucination detection, and the HELM benchmark facilitates future research in this area.
papers.key_findings:
MIND outperforms existing hallucination detection methods in terms of AUC and correlation.
MIND is highly efficient, taking only about 3% of the LLM's response generation time for detection.
Customized training data generated by the same LLM significantly improves hallucination detection performance.
The method is broadly effective across a variety of LLMs.
Using the contextualized embedding of the last token of the last layer is effective for hallucination detection.
papers.limitation: Detecting hallucinations using only the internal states of LLMs may not be as accurate as combining internal states with generated text.
future_direction: Integrating internal states of LLMs with generated text for improved hallucination detection.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models (LLMs) refer to the phenomenon of LLMs producing responses that are coherent yet factually inaccurate. This issue undermines the effectiveness of LLMs in practical applications, necessitating research into detecting and mitigating hallucinations of LLMs. Previous studies have mainly concentrated on post-processing techniques for hallucination detection, which tend to be computationally intensive and limited in effectiveness due to their separation from the LLM's inference process. To overcome these limitations, we introduce MIND, an unsupervised training framework that leverages the internal states of LLMs for real-time hallucination detection without requiring manual annotations. Additionally, we present HELM, a new benchmark for evaluating hallucination detection across multiple LLMs, featuring diverse LLM outputs and the internal states of LLMs during their inference process. Our experiments demonstrate that MIND outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in hallucination detection.

papers.title: SAVE: Sparse Autoencoder-Driven Visual Information Enhancement for Mitigating Object Hallucination
papers.research_question: How can object hallucination in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) be mitigated by using sparse autoencoders to identify and steer along visual understanding features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes SA VE, a framework that uses sparse autoencoders to identify visual understanding features in MLLMs and steers the model along these features to mitigate object hallucination, outperforming training-free baselines.
papers.conclusion: SA VE effectively mitigates object hallucination in MLLMs by steering along visual understanding features identified via sparse autoencoders, demonstrating consistent improvements across models and benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features can be used to identify visual understanding features that are discriminative between correct and hallucinated responses.
Steering along visual understanding features reduces object hallucination, while steering along hallucinated features amplifies it.
SA VE outperforms state-of-the-art training-free methods on CHAIR, POPE, and MMHal-Bench benchmarks.
Steering suppresses the probability of uncertain object tokens and increases attention to image tokens.
The method is robust across different MLLM architectures and layers.
papers.abstract: Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have advanced substantially, they remain vulnerable to object hallucination caused by language priors and visual information loss. To address this, we propose SAVE (Sparse Autoencoder-Driven Visual Information Enhancement), a framework that mitigates hallucination by steering the model along Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) latent features. A binary object-presence question-answering probe identifies the SAE features most indicative of the model's visual information processing, referred to as visual understanding features. Steering the model along these identified features reinforces grounded visual understanding and effectively reduces hallucination. With its simple design, SAVE outperforms state-of-the-art training-free methods on standard benchmarks, achieving a 10\%p improvement in CHAIR\_S and consistent gains on POPE and MMHal-Bench. Extensive evaluations across multiple models and layers confirm the robustness and generalizability of our approach. Further analysis reveals that steering along visual understanding features suppresses the generation of uncertain object tokens and increases attention to image tokens, mitigating hallucination. Code is released at https://github.com/wiarae/SAVE.

papers.title: Steering LVLMs via Sparse Autoencoder for Hallucination Mitigation
papers.research_question: How can we identify and steer semantic directions in LVLMs to mitigate hallucinations using sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes SSL, a plug-and-play method that uses SAE to identify hallucinatory and faithful semantic directions in LVLMs and steers the model during inference to mitigate hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: SSL effectively mitigates hallucinations in LVLMs by steering internal representations and shows transferability across models.
papers.key_findings:
SAE can identify latent directions correlated with hallucinatory and faithful semantics in LVLMs.
Interventions along the faithful direction reduce hallucinations, while interventions along the hallucinatory direction increase them.
SSL outperforms existing decoding methods in reducing hallucinations with negligible time overhead.
The identified semantic directions generalize across different model architectures.
papers.limitation: The only open-source multimodal SAE is trained on LLaVA-NeXT, so the study cannot compare SAEs across different model architectures.
future_direction: Training multimodal SAEs on various architectures to investigate generalization of the findings.
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have achieved remarkable performance on multimodal tasks. However, they still suffer from hallucinations, generating text inconsistent with visual input, posing significant risks in real-world applications. Existing approaches to address this issue focus on incorporating external knowledge bases, alignment training, or decoding strategies, all of which require substantial computational cost and time. Recent works try to explore more efficient alternatives by adjusting LVLMs' internal representations. Although promising, these methods may cause hallucinations to be insufficiently suppressed or lead to excessive interventions that negatively affect normal semantics. In this work, we leverage sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to identify semantic directions closely associated with faithfulness or hallucination, extracting more precise and disentangled hallucination-related representations. Our analysis demonstrates that interventions along the identified faithful direction can mitigate hallucinations, while those along the hallucinatory direction can exacerbate them. Building on these insights, we propose Steering LVLMs via SAE Latent Directions (SSL), a plug-and-play method based on SAE-derived latent directions to mitigate hallucinations in LVLMs. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SSL significantly outperforms existing decoding approaches in mitigating hallucinations, while maintaining transferability across different model architectures with negligible additional time overhead. The code is available at https://github.com/huazhenglin2003/SSL.

papers.title: Toward Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoder (SAE) features capture interpretable signals predictive of hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and how can they be used to build an accurate and interpretable detector?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RAGLens, a lightweight hallucination detector for RAG that uses sparse autoencoder (SAE) features from LLM internal activations, achieving superior detection performance and providing interpretable rationales for its decisions.
papers.conclusion: RAGLens demonstrates that SAE features effectively capture hallucination signals in RAG, enabling accurate, interpretable, and lightweight detection that can generalize across models and tasks.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features capture nuanced signals specifically activated during RAG hallucinations.
RAGLens outperforms existing methods in detection accuracy on multiple benchmarks and models.
The detector provides interpretable rationales via feature attribution and shape functions, enabling post-hoc mitigation.
RAGLens generalizes across different LLMs and RAG task domains.
Mid-layer SAE features with high mutual information about the labels are most informative for detecting RAG hallucinations.
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves the factuality of large language models (LLMs) by grounding outputs in retrieved evidence, but faithfulness failures, where generations contradict or extend beyond the provided sources, remain a critical challenge. Existing hallucination detection methods for RAG often rely either on large-scale detector training, which requires substantial annotated data, or on querying external LLM judges, which leads to high inference costs. Although some approaches attempt to leverage internal representations of LLMs for hallucination detection, their accuracy remains limited. Motivated by recent advances in mechanistic interpretability, we employ sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to disentangle internal activations, successfully identifying features that are specifically triggered during RAG hallucinations. Building on a systematic pipeline of information-based feature selection and additive feature modeling, we introduce RAGLens, a lightweight hallucination detector that accurately flags unfaithful RAG outputs using LLM internal representations. RAGLens not only achieves superior detection performance compared to existing methods, but also provides interpretable rationales for its decisions, enabling effective post-hoc mitigation of unfaithful RAG. Finally, we justify our design choices and reveal new insights into the distribution of hallucination-related signals within LLMs. The code is available at https://github.com/Teddy-XiongGZ/RAGLens.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Learn Monosemantic Features in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be applied to Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to improve interpretability and steerability, and how can we quantitatively evaluate the monosemanticity of neurons in such models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the MonoSemanticity score (MS) to evaluate neuron-level monosemanticity in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), validates MS with a human study, and demonstrates that SAEs can steer multimodal LLM outputs by intervening on vision encoder neurons.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) effectively improve neuron-level monosemanticity in Vision-Language Models, with the MonoSemanticity score providing a reliable metric aligned with human judgment, and shows that SAEs enable unsupervised concept-based steering of multimodal LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs significantly increase the monosemanticity of individual neurons in VLMs compared to original neurons.
Sparsity and wider latent dimensions are the most influential factors for improving monosemanticity.
Matryoshka SAEs achieve overall superior monosemanticity scores compared to standard SAE variants.
SAE interventions on the vision encoder can steer multimodal LLM (e.g., LLaVA) outputs to insert or suppress specific concepts without modifying the language model.
The proposed MonoSemanticity score aligns well with human perception of similarity, as validated by a large-scale user study.
papers.limitation:
High MS score neurons do not always produce precise effects when used to steer MLLM outputs; for example, a 'golden retriever' neuron might trigger any dog-related output due to limited fine-grained understanding in MLLMs.
A fraction of SAE neurons that act as feature detectors do not exhibit any clear steering effect.
future_direction: Adapting the MonoSemanticity metric to text representations.
Investigating the interplay between specialized (low-level) and broad (high-level) concepts within learned representations.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently gained attention as a means to improve the interpretability and steerability of Large Language Models (LLMs), both of which are essential for AI safety. In this work, we extend the application of SAEs to Vision-Language Models (VLMs), such as CLIP, and introduce a comprehensive framework for evaluating monosemanticity at the neuron-level in visual representations. To ensure that our evaluation aligns with human perception, we propose a benchmark derived from a large-scale user study. Our experimental results reveal that SAEs trained on VLMs significantly enhance the monosemanticity of individual neurons, with sparsity and wide latents being the most influential factors. Further, we demonstrate that applying SAE interventions on CLIP's vision encoder directly steers multimodal LLM outputs (e.g., LLaVA), without any modifications to the underlying language model. These findings emphasize the practicality and efficacy of SAEs as an unsupervised tool for enhancing both interpretability and control of VLMs. Code and benchmark data are available at https://github.com/ExplainableML/sae-for-vlm.

papers.title: SAFE: A Sparse Autoencoder-Based Framework for Robust Query Enrichment and Hallucination Mitigation in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we harness the creative power of LLMs while mitigating their hallucinations by steering the model to leverage its existing knowledge more effectively using Sparse Autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SAFE, a two-stage framework that first detects hallucinations via entropy-based uncertainty estimation and then mitigates them by enriching the query with SAE-derived features, improving accuracy without additional training.
papers.conclusion: SAFE significantly reduces hallucination rates and improves response accuracy by up to 29.45% in a training-free, plug-and-play manner, offering a practical solution for enhancing LLM reliability.
papers.key_findings:
SAFE improves accuracy on hallucination-prone QA datasets across different models and architectures.
Ablation studies confirm the critical role of entropy-based detection and SAE-driven enrichment in achieving performance gains.
SAFE can make smaller models perform comparably to larger ones in some cases, as shown by the comparison with Gemma2-27b and Llama3-70b.
The framework operates in a training-free manner, offering a lightweight, plug-and-play solution.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on an SAE and the availability of auto-interpretable features constrains its applicability to LLMs that expose such internal representations.
Effectiveness is influenced by the quality of the input queries.
Current implementation is restricted to English-language inputs.
future_direction: Extending the approach to models without SAE characteristics would require modifications or alternative interpretability techniques.
Multilingual and multimodal extensions are promising directions for future research.
papers.abstract: Despite the state-of-the-art performance of Large Language Models (LLMs), these models often suffer from hallucinations, which can undermine their performance in critical applications. In this work, we propose SAFE, a novel method for detecting and mitigating hallucinations by leveraging Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). While hallucination detection techniques and SAEs have been explored independently, their synergistic application in a comprehensive system, particularly for hallucination-aware query enrichment, has not been fully investigated. To validate the effectiveness of SAFE, we evaluate it on two models with available SAEs across three diverse cross-domain datasets designed to assess hallucination problems. Empirical results demonstrate that SAFE consistently improves query generation accuracy and mitigates hallucinations across all datasets, achieving accuracy improvements of up to 29.45%.

papers.title: LLM Internal States Reveal Hallucination Risk Faced With a Query
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs can estimate their own hallucination risk before response generation using internal states.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLM internal states can indicate whether a query was seen in training data and predict hallucination risk, achieving high accuracy with a probing estimator.
papers.conclusion: This work demonstrates that LLMs have latent self-assessment capabilities to estimate hallucination risks prior to response generation.
papers.key_findings:
Internal states can distinguish seen/unseen queries with 80.28% accuracy.
Internal states can estimate hallucination risk with 84.32% accuracy across 15 NLG tasks.
Layer depth positively correlates with prediction performance.
Internal states are model-specific but allow some zero-shot transfer.
Features in internal states are shared within tasks but not across tasks.
papers.limitation:
Lack of human evaluation in data labeling process.
Trade-off in performance compared to methods using both query and response.
papers.abstract: The hallucination problem of Large Language Models (LLMs) significantly limits their reliability and trustworthiness. Humans have a self-awareness process that allows us to recognize what we don't know when faced with queries. Inspired by this, our paper investigates whether LLMs can estimate their own hallucination risk before response generation. We analyze the internal mechanisms of LLMs broadly both in terms of training data sources and across 15 diverse Natural Language Generation (NLG) tasks, spanning over 700 datasets. Our empirical analysis reveals two key insights: (1) LLM internal states indicate whether they have seen the query in training data or not; and (2) LLM internal states show they are likely to hallucinate or not regarding the query. Our study explores particular neurons, activation layers, and tokens that play a crucial role in the LLM perception of uncertainty and hallucination risk. By a probing estimator, we leverage LLM self-assessment, achieving an average hallucination estimation accuracy of 84.32\% at run time.

papers.title: Prompt-Guided Internal States for Hallucination Detection of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we enhance the cross-domain performance of supervised detectors with only in-domain data?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes PRISM, a framework that uses prompt-guided internal states to enhance the cross-domain generalization of hallucination detectors by making truthfulness structure more salient and consistent.
papers.conclusion: Suitable prompts enhance the salience and consistency of truthfulness structure in LLMs' internal states, and PRISM improves the generalization performance of hallucination detectors.
papers.key_findings:
Introduction of prompts makes the structure related to text truthfulness more salient in LLMs' internal states.
Prompts increase the consistency of truthfulness structure across different domains.
PRISM significantly improves the generalization performance of existing hallucination detection methods.
Variance ratio can effectively guide prompt selection for better performance.
The framework is effective even in real-world scenarios like the TruthfulQA dataset.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on internal states which may be challenging to access, requiring proxy models.
Does not leverage other information like probability information and generated text.
future_direction: Exploring fully utilizing various types of information produced by LLMs during text generation for more effective hallucination detection.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across a variety of tasks in different domains. However, they sometimes generate responses that are logically coherent but factually incorrect or misleading, which is known as LLM hallucinations. Data-driven supervised methods train hallucination detectors by leveraging the internal states of LLMs, but detectors trained on specific domains often struggle to generalize well to other domains. In this paper, we aim to enhance the cross-domain performance of supervised detectors with only in-domain data. We propose a novel framework, prompt-guided internal states for hallucination detection of LLMs, namely PRISM. By utilizing appropriate prompts to guide changes to the structure related to text truthfulness in LLMs' internal states, we make this structure more salient and consistent across texts from different domains. We integrated our framework with existing hallucination detection methods and conducted experiments on datasets from different domains. The experimental results indicate that our framework significantly enhances the cross-domain generalization of existing hallucination detection methods.

papers.title: HARP: Hallucination Detection via Reasoning Subspace Projection
papers.research_question: Can the hidden state space of LLMs be decomposed into semantic and reasoning subspaces, and can projecting onto the reasoning subspace improve hallucination detection?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes HARP, a hallucination detection method that projects hidden states onto a reasoning subspace derived via SVD on the unembedding layer, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
papers.conclusion: HARP is an effective and robust method for hallucination detection by leveraging reasoning subspace projection, demonstrating superior accuracy and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
The hidden state space of LLMs can be decomposed into a direct sum of a semantic subspace and a reasoning subspace.
The Unembedding layer can disentangle these subspaces, and SVD on its parameters yields basis vectors for each.
Projecting hidden states onto the reasoning subspace reduces feature dimension to ~5% of the original, filtering noise and improving robustness.
HARP outperforms existing hallucination detection methods across multiple datasets and models.
A reasoning subspace dimension of about 5% of the hidden state dimension yields optimal detection performance.
future_direction: Hallucination mitigation by modifying reasoning subspace components.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) pose a major barrier to their reliable use in critical decision-making. Although existing hallucination detection methods have improved accuracy, they still struggle with disentangling semantic and reasoning information and maintaining robustness. To address these challenges, we propose HARP (Hallucination detection via reasoning subspace projection), a novel hallucination detection framework. HARP establishes that the hidden state space of LLMs can be decomposed into a direct sum of a semantic subspace and a reasoning subspace, where the former encodes linguistic expression and the latter captures internal reasoning processes. Moreover, we demonstrate that the Unembedding layer can disentangle these subspaces, and by applying Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to its parameters, the basis vectors spanning the semantic and reasoning subspaces are obtained. Finally, HARP projects hidden states onto the basis vectors of the reasoning subspace, and the resulting projections are then used as input features for hallucination detection in LLMs. By using these projections, HARP reduces the dimension of the feature to approximately 5% of the original, filters out most noise, and achieves enhanced robustness. Experiments across multiple datasets show that HARP achieves state-of-the-art hallucination detection performance; in particular, it achieves an AUROC of 92.8% on TriviaQA, outperforming the previous best method by 7.5%.

papers.title: Do I Know This Entity? Knowledge Awareness and Hallucinations in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms behind hallucinations in language models, specifically regarding entity recognition and knowledge awareness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers entity recognition directions in the representation space that encode knowledge awareness and shows they causally affect knowledge refusal and hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models have internal representations of knowledge awareness that affect refusal and hallucinations, and that chat fine-tuning repurposes this existing mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders uncover directions in the representation space that detect whether the model recognizes an entity as known or unknown.
These entity recognition directions generalize across diverse entity types (players, movies, cities, songs).
The directions causally affect knowledge refusal: steering can induce the model to refuse on known entities or hallucinate on unknown entities.
The directions disrupt the attention of downstream heads in the factual recall circuit, suppressing attribute extraction.
Early entity recognition directions regulate the model's expression of knowledge uncertainty, and uncertainty directions are predictive of incorrect answers.
papers.limitation: The methodology for labeling entities as known or unknown might introduce inaccuracies, as the model could guess attributes or fail to recall specific attributes while knowing about the entity.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models are a widespread problem, yet the mechanisms behind whether models will hallucinate are poorly understood, limiting our ability to solve this problem. Using sparse autoencoders as an interpretability tool, we discover that a key part of these mechanisms is entity recognition, where the model detects if an entity is one it can recall facts about. Sparse autoencoders uncover meaningful directions in the representation space, these detect whether the model recognizes an entity, e.g. detecting it doesn't know about an athlete or a movie. This suggests that models can have self-knowledge: internal representations about their own capabilities. These directions are causally relevant: capable of steering the model to refuse to answer questions about known entities, or to hallucinate attributes of unknown entities when it would otherwise refuse. We demonstrate that despite the sparse autoencoders being trained on the base model, these directions have a causal effect on the chat model's refusal behavior, suggesting that chat finetuning has repurposed this existing mechanism. Furthermore, we provide an initial exploration into the mechanistic role of these directions in the model, finding that they disrupt the attention of downstream heads that typically move entity attributes to the final token.

papers.title: Probing the Representational Power of Sparse Autoencoders in Vision Models
papers.research_question: How effective are Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for interpreting and steering vision models, and do they provide semantically meaningful features across different vision architectures?
papers.core_contribution: SAEs extract semantically meaningful features from vision models, improve out-of-distribution generalization, and enable semantic steering in diffusion models, establishing SAEs as a valuable interpretability tool for vision.
papers.conclusion: SAE features are semantically meaningful and enhance interpretable understanding across vision encoders, multimodal LLMs, and diffusion models, highlighting SAEs as a unified interpretability tool across diverse vision architectures.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features from vision encoders improve out-of-distribution generalization compared to original embeddings.
SAE features capture hierarchical semantic structures (ontological features) in image encoders.
SAEs enable semantic steering in diffusion models by manipulating text encoder features.
SAEs reveal shared representations across vision and language modalities in LMMs.
Different SAE variants (ReLU, TopK, Gated) show similar trends in reconstruction and sparsity.
papers.limitation:
Findings on multimodal representation overlap in LMMs are preliminary and require future quantitative validation.
Steering Stable Diffusion 3.5 is more challenging due to its complex text encoding architecture.
future_direction: Quantitative validation of multimodal representation overlap in LMMs.
Systematic investigation of how visual representations evolve through LLM layers.
Future application of SAEs in vision models.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a popular tool for interpreting the hidden states of large language models (LLMs). By learning to reconstruct activations from a sparse bottleneck layer, SAEs discover interpretable features from the high-dimensional internal representations of LLMs. Despite their popularity with language models, SAEs remain understudied in the visual domain. In this work, we provide an extensive evaluation the representational power of SAEs for vision models using a broad range of image-based tasks. Our experimental results demonstrate that SAE features are semantically meaningful, improve out-of-distribution generalization, and enable controllable generation across three vision model architectures: vision embedding models, multi-modal LMMs and diffusion models. In vision embedding models, we find that learned SAE features can be used for OOD detection and provide evidence that they recover the ontological structure of the underlying model. For diffusion models, we demonstrate that SAEs enable semantic steering through text encoder manipulation and develop an automated pipeline for discovering human-interpretable attributes. Finally, we conduct exploratory experiments on multi-modal LLMs, finding evidence that SAE features reveal shared representations across vision and language modalities. Our study provides a foundation for SAE evaluation in vision models, highlighting their strong potential improving interpretability, generalization, and steerability in the visual domain.

papers.title: Hallucination Detection with the Internal Layers of LLMs
papers.research_question: How can a hallucination detection method be built that leverages the internal layers of LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis proposes a new architecture that dynamically weights and combines internal LLM layers to improve hallucination detection performance, though generalization across benchmarks and models remains a challenge.
papers.conclusion: The thesis demonstrates the potential of internal representation analysis for hallucination detection, proposing a method that outperforms baselines but faces generalization challenges. Future work should address these limitations and explore more advanced architectures.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed approach achieves superior performance compared to traditional probing methods on the training benchmark.
Generalization across benchmarks and to other LLMs remains challenging.
Cross-benchmark training and parameter freezing can mitigate generalization limitations in some scenarios, reducing performance degradation when transferred.
The method outperforms implemented baselines (LastLayer, MiddleLayer, StackedLayers, AllLayersEnsemble) on average.
The method did not precisely identify hallucinated spans within text, likely due to high label imbalance.
papers.limitation:
The method does not generalize well across benchmarks and to other LLMs.
The sequential labeling task for identifying hallucinated spans had high label imbalance and did not perform well.
The method requires access to the internal representations of the LLM, which may not be available in all settings.
future_direction: Exploring more advanced architectures for the classifier.
Investigating other comparison methods for layer representations.
Extending the evaluation to other tasks and benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have succeeded in a variety of natural language processing tasks [Zha+25]. However, they have notable limitations. LLMs tend to generate hallucinations, a seemingly plausible yet factually unsupported output [Hua+24], which have serious real-world consequences [Kay23; Rum+24]. Recent work has shown that probing-based classifiers that utilize LLMs' internal representations can detect hallucinations [AM23; Bei+24; Bur+24; DYT24; Ji+24; SMZ24; Su+24]. This approach, since it does not involve model training, can enhance reliability without significantly increasing computational costs. Building upon this approach, this thesis proposed novel methods for hallucination detection using LLM internal representations and evaluated them across three benchmarks: TruthfulQA, HaluEval, and ReFact. Specifically, a new architecture that dynamically weights and combines internal LLM layers was developed to improve hallucination detection performance. Throughout extensive experiments, two key findings were obtained: First, the proposed approach was shown to achieve superior performance compared to traditional probing methods, though generalization across benchmarks and LLMs remains challenging. Second, these generalization limitations were demonstrated to be mitigated through cross-benchmark training and parameter freezing. While not consistently improving, both techniques yielded better performance on individual benchmarks and reduced performance degradation when transferred to other benchmarks. These findings open new avenues for improving LLM reliability through internal representation analysis.

papers.title: ICR Probe: Tracking Hidden State Dynamics for Reliable Hallucination Detection in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can hallucination detection in LLMs be improved by analyzing the dynamic evolution of hidden states across layers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the ICR Score to quantify module contributions to hidden state updates and the ICR Probe, a method for hallucination detection that captures cross-layer residual stream dynamics.
papers.conclusion: The ICR Probe provides an effective and interpretable approach for hallucination detection by focusing on dynamic hidden state updates, with demonstrated superiority over baselines.
papers.key_findings:
ICR Probe outperforms existing hallucination detection methods across multiple datasets and models.
The ICR Score shows consistent patterns across layers and effectively distinguishes hallucinated from non-hallucinated outputs.
Ablation studies reveal that middle layers are most critical for detection.
The method generalizes well across different datasets with minimal performance drop.
Token-level analysis shows that key tokens are more reliably detected than common tokens.
papers.limitation:
Applicable only to open-source models requiring access to hidden states.
Does not directly address mitigating hallucinations in LLMs.
Evaluation limited to current datasets; needs extension to more complex tasks.
future_direction: Explore interventions in the residual stream update process to reduce hallucinations.
Extend evaluations to more complex generation tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at various natural language processing tasks, but their tendency to generate hallucinations undermines their reliability. Existing hallucination detection methods leveraging hidden states predominantly focus on static and isolated representations, overlooking their dynamic evolution across layers, which limits efficacy. To address this limitation, we shift the focus to the hidden state update process and introduce a novel metric, the ICR Score (Information Contribution to Residual Stream), which quantifies the contribution of modules to the hidden states' update. We empirically validate that the ICR Score is effective and reliable in distinguishing hallucinations. Building on these insights, we propose a hallucination detection method, the ICR Probe, which captures the cross-layer evolution of hidden states. Experimental results show that the ICR Probe achieves superior performance with significantly fewer parameters. Furthermore, ablation studies and case analyses offer deeper insights into the underlying mechanism of this method, improving its interpretability.

papers.title: Beyond Logit Lens: Contextual Embeddings for Robust Hallucination Detection & Grounding in VLMs
papers.research_question: What are the limitations of the logit lens for hallucination detection in VLMs, and how can contextual embeddings from middle layers improve detection and grounding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ContextualLens, a training-free method that uses contextual embeddings from middle layers of VLMs to improve hallucination detection and grounding, overcoming limitations of the logit lens.
papers.conclusion: ContextualLens leverages contextual embeddings to enhance hallucination detection and grounding in VLMs, providing a reliable and interpretable method without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
ContextualLens significantly improves hallucination detection in categories like attributes, comparisons, and relations where logit lens performs poorly.
The method enables transition from zero-shot object segmentation to grounded visual question answering with precise bounding boxes.
Contextual embeddings from middle layers are more effective for multi-token concepts and contextual understanding.
papers.limitation:
Validation conducted primarily on factual short answer VQA datasets, limiting generalization to more diverse and complex datasets.
ContextualLens is outperformed by output probabilities in the Count category.
While precise, the bounding box method has lower recall, indicating room for improvement in evidence coverage.
future_direction: Extending validation to more diverse and complex datasets beyond factual short answer VQA.
Exploring extensions to the method for abstractive scenarios such as counting.
Improving recall by leveraging scoring mechanisms as priors for pre-trained segmentation models or enhancing evaluation metrics.
papers.abstract: The rapid development of Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) has significantly advanced multimodal understanding by harnessing the language abilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) and integrating modality-specific encoders. However, LMMs are plagued by hallucinations that limit their reliability and adoption. While traditional methods to detect and mitigate these hallucinations often involve costly training or rely heavily on external models, recent approaches utilizing internal model features present a promising alternative. In this paper, we critically assess the limitations of the state-of-the-art training-free technique, the logit lens, in handling generalized visual hallucinations. We introduce ContextualLens, a refined method that leverages contextual token embeddings from middle layers of LMMs. This approach significantly improves hallucination detection and grounding across diverse categories, including actions and OCR, while also excelling in tasks requiring contextual understanding, such as spatial relations and attribute comparison. Our novel grounding technique yields highly precise bounding boxes, facilitating a transition from Zero-Shot Object Segmentation to Grounded Visual Question Answering. Our contributions pave the way for more reliable and interpretable multimodal models.

papers.title: Towards Principled Evaluations of Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Control
papers.research_question: How to evaluate sparse autoencoders for interpretability and control in the context of specific tasks, by comparing them against supervised feature dictionaries.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework for evaluating sparse autoencoders using supervised feature dictionaries as a benchmark, applied to the IOI task.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides a step towards more objective evaluations of sparse dictionary learning methods.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs capture interpretable features for the IOI task but are less successful than supervised features in controlling the model.
Feature occlusion and feature over-splitting phenomena are observed in SAE training.
papers.limitation: The F1 score does not take into account the magnitude of feature activations and is a conservative metric.
future_direction: Address limitations of the F1 score in interpretability evaluations
papers.abstract: Disentangling model activations into meaningful features is a central problem in interpretability. However, the absence of ground-truth for these features in realistic scenarios makes validating recent approaches, such as sparse dictionary learning, elusive. To address this challenge, we propose a framework for evaluating feature dictionaries in the context of specific tasks, by comparing them against \emph{supervised} feature dictionaries. First, we demonstrate that supervised dictionaries achieve excellent approximation, control, and interpretability of model computations on the task. Second, we use the supervised dictionaries to develop and contextualize evaluations of unsupervised dictionaries along the same three axes. We apply this framework to the indirect object identification (IOI) task using GPT-2 Small, with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on either the IOI or OpenWebText datasets. We find that these SAEs capture interpretable features for the IOI task, but they are less successful than supervised features in controlling the model. Finally, we observe two qualitative phenomena in SAE training: feature occlusion (where a causally relevant concept is robustly overshadowed by even slightly higher-magnitude ones in the learned features), and feature over-splitting (where binary features split into many smaller, less interpretable features). We hope that our framework will provide a useful step towards more objective and grounded evaluations of sparse dictionary learning methods.

papers.title: ReDeEP: Detecting Hallucination in Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms behind hallucinations in retrieval-augmented generation scenarios, and how can they be detected?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ReDeEP, a method for detecting RAG hallucinations by analyzing LLMs' use of external context and parametric knowledge through mechanistic interpretability.
papers.conclusion: ReDeEP demonstrates significant performance improvements across the LLaMA family and RAG hallucination benchmarks, outperforming existing detection methods.
papers.key_findings:
Hallucinations occur when Knowledge FFNs overemphasize parametric knowledge in the residual stream.
Copying Heads fail to effectively retain or integrate external knowledge from retrieved content.
There is a causal relationship between Knowledge FFNs, Copying Heads, and RAG hallucinations.
ReDeEP significantly improves hallucination detection accuracy by decoupling external and parametric knowledge utilization.
AARF mitigates hallucinations by modulating the contributions of Knowledge FFNs and Copying Heads without updating model parameters.
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models are designed to incorporate external knowledge, reducing hallucinations caused by insufficient parametric (internal) knowledge. However, even with accurate and relevant retrieved content, RAG models can still produce hallucinations by generating outputs that conflict with the retrieved information. Detecting such hallucinations requires disentangling how Large Language Models (LLMs) utilize external and parametric knowledge. Current detection methods often focus on one of these mechanisms or without decoupling their intertwined effects, making accurate detection difficult. In this paper, we investigate the internal mechanisms behind hallucinations in RAG scenarios. We discover hallucinations occur when the Knowledge FFNs in LLMs overemphasize parametric knowledge in the residual stream, while Copying Heads fail to effectively retain or integrate external knowledge from retrieved content. Based on these findings, we propose ReDeEP, a novel method that detects hallucinations by decoupling LLM's utilization of external context and parametric knowledge. Our experiments show that ReDeEP significantly improves RAG hallucination detection accuracy. Additionally, we introduce AARF, which mitigates hallucinations by modulating the contributions of Knowledge FFNs and Copying Heads.

papers.title: Exploring Causes and Mitigation of Hallucinations in Large Vision Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the causes of hallucinations in Large Vision Language Models during image captioning, and how can they be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to detect and reduce hallucinations in LVLMs by comparing token-level hidden representations from inference passes with and without the image, training a classifier on this difference, and using it to guide a novel decoding strategy.
papers.conclusion: Hallucinations in LVLMs arise as language priors override visual information during generation; the proposed method using hidden state differences effectively reduces these hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Hallucinations are more likely to occur in the later parts of generated captions.
LVLMs show inconsistent object recognition between generative and discriminative tasks.
Token probability distributions are highly similar with and without image input, indicating heavy reliance on language priors.
A classifier trained on the difference between hidden states with and without the image can effectively predict token-level hallucinations.
The proposed decoding strategy using this classifier significantly reduces hallucination rates in image captioning.
papers.limitation:
The approach may penalize cases where the description of visual content naturally aligns with statistical patterns learned from training data.
The implementation uses basic vector subtraction without exploring more sophisticated distance metrics.
The classifier is highly model-specific and task-dependent, limiting its applicability to other models or tasks.
The token-level classifier was trained with sentence-level annotations, reducing its ability to make fine-grained judgments about hallucinated content.
future_direction: Developing generalized end-to-end solutions to address hallucinations in LVLMs beyond image captioning.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) integrate image encoders with Large Language Models (LLMs) to process multi-modal inputs and perform complex visual tasks. However, they often generate hallucinations by describing non-existent objects or attributes, compromising their reliability. This study analyzes hallucination patterns in image captioning, showing that not all tokens in the generation process are influenced by image input and that image dependency can serve as a useful signal for hallucination detection. To address this, we develop an automated pipeline to identify hallucinated objects and train a token-level classifier using hidden representations from parallel inference passes-with and without image input. Leveraging this classifier, we introduce a decoding strategy that effectively controls hallucination rates in image captioning at inference time.

papers.title: The Missing Curve Detectors of InceptionV1: Applying Sparse Autoencoders to InceptionV1 Early Vision
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders uncover interpretable features and address polysemantic neurons in InceptionV1's early vision layers?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable features from InceptionV1, revealing missing curve detectors and decomposing polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic features.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are a valuable tool for understanding InceptionV1 and convolutional neural networks, extending their promise beyond language models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs learn new interpretable features that were not visible when examining individual neurons.
SAEs discover additional curve detector features that fill gaps in the known family of curve detectors.
SAEs can split polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic constituent features.
papers.limitation: This paper is a very early report and does not defend the results in a systematic way.
future_direction: Investigate branch specialization and cross-branch superposition in InceptionV1 using SAEs.
papers.abstract: Recent work on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) has shown promise in extracting interpretable features from neural networks and addressing challenges with polysemantic neurons caused by superposition. In this paper, we apply SAEs to the early vision layers of InceptionV1, a well-studied convolutional neural network, with a focus on curve detectors. Our results demonstrate that SAEs can uncover new interpretable features not apparent from examining individual neurons, including additional curve detectors that fill in previous gaps. We also find that SAEs can decompose some polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic constituent features. These findings suggest SAEs are a valuable tool for understanding InceptionV1, and convolutional neural networks more generally.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Layer-wise Semantic Dynamics for Hallucination Detection in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can hallucinations in Large Language Models be detected by analyzing the geometric evolution of hidden-state semantics across transformer layers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Layer-wise Semantic Dynamics (LSD), a geometric framework for hallucination detection that analyzes the evolution of hidden-state semantics across transformer layers, achieving high performance with a single forward pass.
papers.conclusion: LSD provides a scalable, model-agnostic framework for real-time hallucination detection that bridges empirical detection and theoretical understanding by revealing the geometric signatures of truth within neural representations.
papers.key_findings:
Factual and hallucinated content follow distinct geometric trajectories: factual responses show stable convergence toward truth embeddings, while hallucinations exhibit oscillatory divergence.
LSD achieves an F1-score of 0.92 and AUROC of 0.96 on TruthfulQA, outperforming baselines like SelfCheckGPT and Semantic Entropy.
The method requires only a single forward pass, yielding a 5–20× speedup over sampling-based methods.
Alignment-based metrics (e.g., Final Alignment) show extremely large effect sizes (Cohen's d > 2.8) and high statistical significance (p < 10^-10) between factual and hallucinated distributions.
The semantic alignment projection component is most critical, with its removal causing a 28% performance drop.
papers.limitation:
Performance partially depends on the quality of the external truth encoder.
Layer-wise extraction adds memory burden.
Currently limited to textual content.
future_direction: Explore encoder-free variants.
Develop efficient approximations.
Extend to multimodal content.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often produce fluent yet factually incorrect statements-a phenomenon known as hallucination-posing serious risks in high-stakes domains. We present Layer-wise Semantic Dynamics (LSD), a geometric framework for hallucination detection that analyzes the evolution of hidden-state semantics across transformer layers. Unlike prior methods that rely on multiple sampling passes or external verification sources, LSD operates intrinsically within the model's representational space. Using margin-based contrastive learning, LSD aligns hidden activations with ground-truth embeddings derived from a factual encoder, revealing a distinct separation in semantic trajectories: factual responses preserve stable alignment, while hallucinations exhibit pronounced semantic drift across depth. Evaluated on the TruthfulQA and synthetic factual-hallucination datasets, LSD achieves an F1-score of 0.92, AUROC of 0.96, and clustering accuracy of 0.89, outperforming SelfCheckGPT and Semantic Entropy baselines while requiring only a single forward pass. This efficiency yields a 5-20x speedup over sampling-based methods without sacrificing precision or interpretability. LSD offers a scalable, model-agnostic mechanism for real-time hallucination monitoring and provides new insights into the geometry of factual consistency within large language models.

papers.title: Data-efficient Meta-models for Evaluation of Context-based Questions and Answers in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can training data requirements be reduced for state-of-the-art hallucination detection frameworks while maintaining competitive performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a data-efficient framework for hallucination detection that combines feature extraction from LLM internals with lightweight classifiers, achieving competitive performance with only 250 training samples.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that lightweight, annotation-efficient approaches can achieve competitive performance for hallucination detection in industrial settings, overcoming constraints of limited data, computational cost, and privacy.
papers.key_findings:
Lightweight methods using internal LLM states can achieve competitive hallucination detection performance with limited training data.
TabPFNv2 is the top-performing meta-classifier in low-data settings, outperforming logistic regression and CatBoost on average.
PCA dimensionality reduction often enhances the performance of lookback features compared to UMAP or raw features.
Performance improves sharply with 50-250 training samples and plateaus thereafter, demonstrating high data-efficiency.
The choice of extractor LLM affects detector performance, with Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B generally outperforming Gemma-2-9B.
future_direction: Explore architectural modifications of tabular foundation models like TabPFNv2 for NLP representation learning and hallucination detection tasks.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are increasingly deployed in industry applications, yet their reliability remains hampered by challenges in detecting hallucinations. While supervised state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods that leverage LLM hidden states -- such as activation tracing and representation analysis -- show promise, their dependence on extensively annotated datasets limits scalability in real-world applications. This paper addresses the critical bottleneck of data annotation by investigating the feasibility of reducing training data requirements for two SOTA hallucination detection frameworks: Lookback Lens, which analyzes attention head dynamics, and probing-based approaches, which decode internal model representations. We propose a methodology combining efficient classification algorithms with dimensionality reduction techniques to minimize sample size demands while maintaining competitive performance. Evaluations on standardized question-answering RAG benchmarks show that our approach achieves performance comparable to strong proprietary LLM-based baselines with only 250 training samples. These results highlight the potential of lightweight, data-efficient paradigms for industrial deployment, particularly in annotation-constrained scenarios.

papers.title: Sparse but Wrong: Incorrect L0 Leads to Incorrect Features in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How does the L0 hyperparameter (average number of active features per token) in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) affect the quality of learned features, and how can the correct L0 be determined?
papers.core_contribution: The L0 hyperparameter in Sparse Autoencoders must be set correctly to learn monosemantic features; if L0 is too low or too high, the SAE mixes correlated features, and the paper provides a proxy metric (decoder pairwise cosine similarity) to guide L0 selection.
papers.conclusion: The L0 hyperparameter must be set correctly for SAEs to learn correct, monosemantic features, and most existing SAEs likely have an L0 that is too low.
papers.key_findings:
If L0 is set too low, SAEs mix positively correlated features to improve reconstruction, leading to polysemantic latents.
If L0 is set too high, SAEs find degenerate solutions that also mix features.
Commonly used sparsity–reconstruction tradeoff plots are not a sound evaluation method, as they can favor incorrect SAEs that mix features over a ground-truth SAE.
A proxy metric, decoder pairwise cosine similarity (c_dec), is minimized when the SAE L0 matches the true underlying L0 of the data distribution.
Most commonly used open-source SAEs have an L0 that is too low.
papers.limitation:
The investigation is limited to features satisfying the linear representation hypothesis and does not consider non-linear underlying features.
The study only investigated a few layers of popular LLMs due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Investigate how SAEs react if the underlying features are non-linear.
Explore the impact of different correlation structures (e.g., unbalanced correlations) on SAEs.
Extend the analysis to more layers of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) extract features from LLM internal activations, meant to correspond to interpretable concepts. A core SAE training hyperparameter is L0: how many SAE features should fire per token on average. Existing work compares SAE algorithms using sparsity-reconstruction tradeoff plots, implying L0 is a free parameter with no single correct value aside from its effect on reconstruction. In this work we study the effect of L0 on SAEs, and show that if L0 is not set correctly, the SAE fails to disentangle the underlying features of the LLM. If L0 is too low, the SAE will mix correlated features to improve reconstruction. If L0 is too high, the SAE finds degenerate solutions that also mix features. Further, we present a proxy metric that can help guide the search for the correct L0 for an SAE on a given training distribution. We show that our method finds the correct L0 in toy models and coincides with peak sparse probing performance in LLM SAEs. We find that most commonly used SAEs have an L0 that is too low. Our work shows that L0 must be set correctly to train SAEs with correct features.

papers.title: Taming Polysemanticity in LLMs: Provable Feature Recovery via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How to formulate a statistical model for feature recovery in polysemantic LLM representations, and design an SAE training algorithm with provable recovery guarantees and practical effectiveness.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a statistical framework for feature recovery in polysemantic LLM representations and proposes Group Bias Adaptation (GBA), an SAE training algorithm with provable recovery guarantees and improved empirical performance.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a statistical framework and the GBA algorithm for provable feature recovery in SAEs, advancing mechanistic interpretability with theoretical guarantees and empirical improvements.
papers.key_findings:
Proposes a statistical model that formalizes polysemantic features as sparse mixtures of underlying monosemantic concepts.
Introduces Group Bias Adaptation (GBA), an SAE training algorithm that uses bias adaptation to control neuron sparsity without hyperparameter tuning.
Provides the first provable recovery guarantee for an SAE algorithm, showing GBA recovers all monosemantic features under the statistical model.
Empirically demonstrates GBA achieves superior sparsity-loss trade-off and feature consistency on LLMs up to 1.5B parameters compared to baseline methods.
future_direction: Extending the statistical framework to more complex data distributions.
Scaling GBA to larger models.
Exploring applications in model steering and control.
papers.abstract: We study the challenge of achieving theoretically grounded feature recovery using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for the interpretation of Large Language Models. Existing SAE training algorithms often lack rigorous mathematical guarantees and suffer from practical limitations such as hyperparameter sensitivity and instability. To address these issues, we first propose a novel statistical framework for the feature recovery problem, which includes a new notion of feature identifiability by modeling polysemantic features as sparse mixtures of underlying monosemantic concepts. Building on this framework, we introduce a new SAE training algorithm based on ``bias adaptation'', a technique that adaptively adjusts neural network bias parameters to ensure appropriate activation sparsity. We theoretically \highlight{prove that this algorithm correctly recovers all monosemantic features} when input data is sampled from our proposed statistical model. Furthermore, we develop an improved empirical variant, Group Bias Adaptation (GBA), and \highlight{demonstrate its superior performance against benchmark methods when applied to LLMs with up to 1.5 billion parameters}. This work represents a foundational step in demystifying SAE training by providing the first SAE algorithm with theoretical recovery guarantees, thereby advancing the development of more transparent and trustworthy AI systems through enhanced mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Interpretable and Steerable Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the interpretability and steerability of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) by incorporating user-specified concepts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders (CB-SAE), a framework that prunes low-utility SAE neurons and augments the latent space with a concept bottleneck aligned to user-defined concepts, improving interpretability and steerability.
papers.conclusion: CB-SAE unifies sparse autoencoders with concept bottleneck models, enabling robust interpretation and control of vision representations across modalities and architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Most SAE neurons have low interpretability or steerability, rendering them ineffective for downstream use.
SAEs often fail to represent user-specified concepts, limiting their practical utility.
CB-SAE improves interpretability by +32.1% and steerability by +14.5% over SAE baselines across LVLMs and image generation tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) promise a unified approach for mechanistic interpretability, concept discovery, and model steering in LLMs and LVLMs. However, realizing this potential requires that the learned features be both interpretable and steerable. To that end, we introduce two new computationally inexpensive interpretability and steerability metrics and conduct a systematic analysis on LVLMs. Our analysis uncovers two observations; (i) a majority of SAE neurons exhibit either low interpretability or low steerability or both, rendering them ineffective for downstream use; and (ii) due to the unsupervised nature of SAEs, user-desired concepts are often absent in the learned dictionary, thus limiting their practical utility. To address these limitations, we propose Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders (CB-SAE) - a novel post-hoc framework that prunes low-utility neurons and augments the latent space with a lightweight concept bottleneck aligned to a user-defined concept set. The resulting CB-SAE improves interpretability by +32.1% and steerability by +14.5% across LVLMs and image generation tasks. We will make our code and model weights available.

papers.title: Rethinking Evaluation of Sparse Autoencoders through the Representation of Polysemous Words
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can extract interpretable monosemantic features from polysemantic activations in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes PS-Eval, a new evaluation metric and dataset for assessing whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can extract monosemantic features from polysemantic activations. It finds that SAEs optimized for MSE-L0 Pareto frontier do not necessarily improve monosemantic feature extraction, and that deeper layers and attention mechanisms contribute to distinguishing polysemous words.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes Poly-Semantic Evaluation (PS-Eval), a new metric and dataset to assess the ability of SAEs to extract monosemantic features from polysemantic activations, in complement to traditional MSE or L0 metrics. The work encourages the community to conduct holistic evaluations of SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs developed to improve the MSE-L0 Pareto frontier may confuse interpretability and do not necessarily enhance the extraction of monosemantic features.
Deeper layers and the Attention module contribute to distinguishing polysemy in a word.
Increasing the latent dimension of SAEs generally improves specificity up to a saturation point.
Activation functions like TopK and JumpReLU, designed to improve MSE-L0 trade-off, do not perform well on PS-Eval metrics; ReLU performs best.
SAE features are more interpretable than raw LLM activations for polysemous words.
papers.limitation: PS-Eval relies on evaluating the maximum activation of SAE features, which may not always align with intended word meanings and could introduce ambiguity.
future_direction: Incorporate similarity metrics that utilize the distribution of SAE features, rather than relying solely on maximum activation.
Extend PS-Eval beyond natural language to other domains such as diffusion models and vision-language models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have gained a lot of attention as a promising tool to improve the interpretability of large language models (LLMs) by mapping the complex superposition of polysemantic neurons into monosemantic features and composing a sparse dictionary of words. However, traditional performance metrics like Mean Squared Error and L0 sparsity ignore the evaluation of the semantic representational power of SAEs -- whether they can acquire interpretable monosemantic features while preserving the semantic relationship of words. For instance, it is not obvious whether a learned sparse feature could distinguish different meanings in one word. In this paper, we propose a suite of evaluations for SAEs to analyze the quality of monosemantic features by focusing on polysemous words. Our findings reveal that SAEs developed to improve the MSE-L0 Pareto frontier may confuse interpretability, which does not necessarily enhance the extraction of monosemantic features. The analysis of SAEs with polysemous words can also figure out the internal mechanism of LLMs; deeper layers and the Attention module contribute to distinguishing polysemy in a word. Our semantics focused evaluation offers new insights into the polysemy and the existing SAE objective and contributes to the development of more practical SAEs.

papers.title: From Noise to Narrative: Tracing the Origins of Hallucinations in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do hallucinations arise in pre-trained transformer models, and how can internal concept activations predict them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that pre-trained transformers impose semantic structure on noisy inputs, that the number of activated concepts increases with input uncertainty, and that internal concept activations can predict hallucinations in the output.
papers.conclusion: We have shown that pre-trained transformers impose coherent, steerable conceptual structure even on pure noise or randomly shuffled inputs, with the repertoire of activated concepts expanding as input structure degrades, across both images and text.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers impose semantic structure on ambiguous or noisy inputs, revealing an input-insensitive inductive bias.
The number of semantic concepts activated increases with input uncertainty, especially in middle layers.
Internal concept activations in transformer layers can reliably predict the tendency of the model to hallucinate in its output.
papers.limitation: The linear representation hypothesis may not hold for all features, and our evaluation is limited by the ImageNet dataset.
papers.abstract: As generative AI systems become competent and democratized in science, business, and government, deeper insight into their failure modes now poses an acute need. The occasional volatility in their behavior, such as the propensity of transformer models to hallucinate, impedes trust and adoption of emerging AI solutions in high-stakes areas. In the present work, we establish how and when hallucinations arise in pre-trained transformer models through concept representations captured by sparse autoencoders, under scenarios with experimentally controlled uncertainty in the input space. Our systematic experiments reveal that the number of semantic concepts used by the transformer model grows as the input information becomes increasingly unstructured. In the face of growing uncertainty in the input space, the transformer model becomes prone to activate coherent yet input-insensitive semantic features, leading to hallucinated output. At its extreme, for pure-noise inputs, we identify a wide variety of robustly triggered and meaningful concepts in the intermediate activations of pre-trained transformer models, whose functional integrity we confirm through targeted steering. We also show that hallucinations in the output of a transformer model can be reliably predicted from the concept patterns embedded in transformer layer activations. This collection of insights on transformer internal processing mechanics has immediate consequences for aligning AI models with human values, AI safety, opening the attack surface for potential adversarial attacks, and providing a basis for automatic quantification of a model's hallucination risk.

papers.title: InterpDetect: Interpretable Signals for Detecting Hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.research_question: Can interpretable mechanistic signals (External Context Score and Parametric Knowledge Score) be used to build efficient and generalizable hallucination detectors for Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for detecting hallucinations in RAG by using interpretable mechanistic signals (External Context Score and Parametric Knowledge Score) derived from model internals, which are shown to be effective and generalizable across models.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic signals provide efficient, generalizable predictors for hallucination detection in RAG systems, enabling low-cost evaluation of large-scale models.
papers.key_findings:
Hallucinations in RAG arise when later-layer FFN modules disproportionately inject parametric knowledge into the residual stream while attention underweights retrieved content.
External Context Score (ECS) and Parametric Knowledge Score (PKS) are effective features for training classifiers to detect hallucinated spans in RAG outputs.
Classifiers trained on mechanistic signals extracted from a small model (Qwen3-0.6b) can generalize to detect hallucinations in responses from larger, production-level models (GPT-4.1-mini).
The proposed method achieves competitive performance with commercial detection systems while being more computationally efficient.
The model exhibits higher recall than precision, which is argued to be desirable for downstream verification tasks.
papers.limitation:
Computing ECS and PKS across all layers and heads is computationally intensive, especially during the projection from hidden states to the vocabulary distribution.
The overall detection performance remains below that of large-scale models.
The proxy-based evaluation framework is insufficient for real-time response intervention, which would require access to and manipulation of layer-level activations.
future_direction: Identify the layers most critical for efficient hallucination detection to reduce computation.
Expand the feature set to include uncertainty-based measures and representation-level features to improve detection accuracy.
Apply mechanistic signals for response intervention to produce more reliable and truthful outputs.
