papers.research_question: How can we improve sparse autoencoders to better interpret vision-language models like CLIP by achieving a better trade-off between reconstruction quality and sparsity?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoder (MSAE), a hierarchical SAE architecture that achieves state-of-the-art Pareto frontier between reconstruction quality and sparsity for CLIP, enabling effective interpretation and control via concept extraction.
papers.conclusion: MSAE provides an effective method for interpreting and controlling CLIP through hierarchical sparse autoencoding, with practical applications in concept-based similarity search and bias analysis.
papers.key_findings:
MSAE establishes a new Pareto frontier between reconstruction quality (0.99 cosine similarity, <0.1 FVU) and sparsity (~80%) for CLIP.
MSAE extracts over 120 interpretable semantic concepts from CLIP's representation space, validated across image and text modalities.
MSAE enables concept-based similarity search and bias analysis, demonstrated on downstream tasks like CelebA for gender bias.
papers.limitation: The concept mapping approach has limitations, including potential poor assignments when no good matches exist and challenges with hierarchical concepts due to non-orthogonal semantic feature vectors or incomplete vocabulary coverage.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are useful for detecting and steering interpretable features in neural networks, with particular potential for understanding complex multimodal representations. Given their ability to uncover interpretable features, SAEs are particularly valuable for analyzing large-scale vision-language models (e.g., CLIP and SigLIP), which are fundamental building blocks in modern systems yet remain challenging to interpret and control. However, current SAE methods are limited by optimizing both reconstruction quality and sparsity simultaneously, as they rely on either activation suppression or rigid sparsity constraints. To this end, we introduce Matryoshka SAE (MSAE), a new architecture that learns hierarchical representations at multiple granularities simultaneously, enabling a direct optimization of both metrics without compromise. MSAE establishes a new state-of-the-art Pareto frontier between reconstruction quality and sparsity for CLIP, achieving 0.99 cosine similarity and less than 0.1 fraction of variance unexplained while maintaining ~80% sparsity. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of MSAE as a tool for interpreting and controlling CLIP by extracting over 120 semantic concepts from its representation to perform concept-based similarity search and bias analysis in downstream tasks like CelebA. We make the codebase available at https://github.com/WolodjaZ/MSAE.

papers.title: Geospatial Mechanistic Interpretability of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally represent and process geographical information?
papers.core_contribution: Establishes a novel framework for geospatial mechanistic interpretability, demonstrating that LLMs' internal representations for geographical information exhibit spatial autocorrelation and can be decomposed into interpretable features using sparse autoencoders.
papers.conclusion: The framework advances the understanding of how LLMs handle geographical information and opens up new research questions in geospatial mechanistic interpretability, contributing to AI safety and reliable geoAI tools.
papers.key_findings:
Internal representations handling geographical information in LLMs are often distributed across polysemantic neurons, consistent with the superposition hypothesis.
Spatial autocorrelation analysis shows that activations for placenames display geospatial patterns, indicating that the model encodes geographical relationships.
Sparse autoencoders can disentangle polysemantic structures into more interpretable, monosemantic features that reveal clearer geospatial patterns.
Features extracted via sparse autoencoders encode specific geographical regions or concepts, such as Wales or southern Italy, and urban areas like New York City and London.
Only a small percentage (0.2%) of features show significant spatial autocorrelation, suggesting that geographical information is sparsely encoded in the model.
papers.limitation:
Placename ambiguity impacts the interpretation and may require further handling.
The scale of geographical relationships encoded and their interaction with other types of relationships remain open questions.
Only a small fraction of features from the sparse autoencoder showed spatial autocorrelation, indicating room for improvement in decomposition methods.
future_direction: Exploring how placename ambiguity impacts LLMs' learning and interpretability.
Investigating what scale(s) of geographical relationships are encoded and at which model depths.
Examining how geographical relationships compare to and interact with other types of relationships (e.g., social, economic, historical).
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated unprecedented capabilities across various natural language processing tasks. Their ability to process and generate viable text and code has made them ubiquitous in many fields, while their deployment as knowledge bases and "reasoning" tools remains an area of ongoing research. In geography, a growing body of literature has been focusing on evaluating LLMs' geographical knowledge and their ability to perform spatial reasoning. However, very little is still known about the internal functioning of these models, especially about how they process geographical information. In this chapter, we establish a novel framework for the study of geospatial mechanistic interpretability - using spatial analysis to reverse engineer how LLMs handle geographical information. Our aim is to advance our understanding of the internal representations that these complex models generate while processing geographical information - what one might call "how LLMs think about geographic information" if such phrasing was not an undue anthropomorphism. We first outline the use of probing in revealing internal structures within LLMs. We then introduce the field of mechanistic interpretability, discussing the superposition hypothesis and the role of sparse autoencoders in disentangling polysemantic internal representations of LLMs into more interpretable, monosemantic features. In our experiments, we use spatial autocorrelation to show how features obtained for placenames display spatial patterns related to their geographic location and can thus be interpreted geospatially, providing insights into how these models process geographical information. We conclude by discussing how our framework can help shape the study and use of foundation models in geography.

papers.title: Finding Neurons in a Haystack: Case Studies with Sparse Probing
papers.research_question: How are high-level human-interpretable features represented within the internal neuron activations of LLMs, and how does the sparsity of these representations vary with model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces sparse probing to localize individual neurons representing features in LLMs, revealing that early layers use superposition (sparse combinations of polysemantic neurons), middle layers have seemingly dedicated neurons for higher-level features, and model scale increases representational sparsity with varied dynamics.
papers.conclusion: Sparse probing is a powerful tool for understanding feature representation in LLMs, revealing superposition in early layers and monosemantic neurons in middle layers, with scaling effects on sparsity, and opens many directions for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers represent many features in superposition via sparse linear combinations of polysemantic neurons.
Middle layers contain seemingly dedicated (monosemantic) neurons for higher-level contextual features like language or code.
Increasing model scale generally increases representational sparsity, but different features exhibit distinct scaling dynamics.
Sparse probing is an effective method for locating interpretable neurons, even when they are in superposition.
There is a tremendous amount of interpretable structure within the neurons of LLMs, accessible through careful probing and analysis.
papers.limitation:
Interpretation of neurons can be misleading due to 'interpretability illusions' from only examining maximum activating examples.
Conclusive statements about monosemanticity remain methodologically out of reach.
future_direction: Apply sparse probing to other model families and architectures.
Study the dynamics of feature representation during training, not just in final models.
Extend sparse probing to multimodal models and other modalities.
papers.abstract: Despite rapid adoption and deployment of large language models (LLMs), the internal computations of these models remain opaque and poorly understood. In this work, we seek to understand how high-level human-interpretable features are represented within the internal neuron activations of LLMs. We train $k$-sparse linear classifiers (probes) on these internal activations to predict the presence of features in the input; by varying the value of $k$ we study the sparsity of learned representations and how this varies with model scale. With $k=1$, we localize individual neurons which are highly relevant for a particular feature, and perform a number of case studies to illustrate general properties of LLMs. In particular, we show that early layers make use of sparse combinations of neurons to represent many features in superposition, that middle layers have seemingly dedicated neurons to represent higher-level contextual features, and that increasing scale causes representational sparsity to increase on average, but there are multiple types of scaling dynamics. In all, we probe for over 100 unique features comprising 10 different categories in 7 different models spanning 70 million to 6.9 billion parameters.

papers.title: Intervene-All-Paths: Unified Mitigation of LVLM Hallucinations across Alignment Formats
papers.research_question: What are the causes of hallucination in LVLMs and how can they be mitigated by intervening on multiple causal pathways?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a comprehensive multi-path intervention framework for mitigating hallucinations in LVLMs, with novel methods to identify critical heads and insights into pathway usage, leading to consistent improvements across benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed AllPath method effectively mitigates hallucinations across diverse benchmarks by intervening on multiple causal pathways, demonstrating the importance of a comprehensive approach.
papers.key_findings:
Hallucinations in LVLMs arise from the interplay of image-to-input-text, image-to-output-text, and text-to-text causal pathways.
Text-to-text intervened heads are highly correlated with the question-answer alignment format.
Image-to-input-text and image-to-output-text heads are distinct, despite both attending to image tokens.
LVLMs adaptively select different causal pathways depending on the question type.
papers.limitation:
Does not investigate which causal pathways are most effective for different question types, nor explore training strategies to improve pathway usage.
Constrained by the scope of existing hallucination benchmarks, which may not capture a broader range of subtle hallucinations.
future_direction: Investigating what causal pathways are most effective for different types of questions.
Exploring training strategies that could systematically improve the use of such pathways.
Extending to a broader range of hallucinations beyond current benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Despite their impressive performance across a wide range of tasks, Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) remain prone to hallucination. In this study, we propose a comprehensive intervention framework aligned with the transformer's causal architecture in LVLMs, integrating the effects of different intervention paths on hallucination. We find that hallucinations in LVLMs do not arise from a single causal path, but rather from the interplay among image-to-input-text, image-to-output-text, and text-to-text pathways. For the first time, we also find that LVLMs rely on different pathways depending on the question-answer alignment format. Building on these insights, we propose simple yet effective methods to identify and intervene on critical hallucination heads within each pathway, tailored to discriminative and generative formats. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently reduces hallucinations across diverse alignment types.

papers.title: Do LLMs Know about Hallucination? An Empirical Investigation of LLM's Hidden States
papers.research_question: Do LLMs possess awareness of hallucination, and if so, to what extent and through what mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Provides empirical evidence that LLMs exhibit awareness of hallucination through differences in hidden states when processing correct vs hallucinated answers, and shows potential for using hidden state guidance to mitigate hallucination.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess awareness of hallucination as evidenced by differences in hidden states, and leveraging hidden state guidance can help mitigate hallucination.
papers.key_findings:
LLM’s final hidden state is more susceptible to be influenced by a correct answer compared to a hallucinated one.
Strategically inducing an LLM to produce hallucinated responses can raise its awareness consequently.
The level of awareness corresponds to the uncertainty of the LLM in the responses.
Providing relevant knowledge can assist LLMs in identifying hallucinated responses.
The transition between hidden states encodes truthfulness information.
papers.limitation:
Do not differentiate between fine-grained categories of hallucination.
Do not examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers, only the final layer.
Experiments are performed on conventional QA tasks, not more complicated or domain-specific tasks.
Future research is needed to develop more effective strategies for mitigating LLM hallucination.
future_direction: Explore different types of hallucination (factual fabrication, instruction inconsistency, etc.).
Examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers and investigate layer-by-layer formation of hallucination.
Adapt the experimental framework to more complicated or domain-specific tasks and potentially extend to multimodal features.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can make up answers that are not real, and this is known as hallucination. This research aims to see if, how, and to what extent LLMs are aware of hallucination. More specifically, we check whether and how an LLM reacts differently in its hidden states when it answers a question right versus when it hallucinates. To do this, we introduce an experimental framework which allows examining LLM's hidden states in different hallucination situations. Building upon this framework, we conduct a series of experiments with language models in the LLaMA family (Touvron et al., 2023). Our empirical findings suggest that LLMs react differently when processing a genuine response versus a fabricated one. We then apply various model interpretation techniques to help understand and explain the findings better. Moreover, informed by the empirical observations, we show great potential of using the guidance derived from LLM's hidden representation space to mitigate hallucination. We believe this work provides insights into how LLMs produce hallucinated answers and how to make them occur less often.

papers.title: Sanity Checks for Sparse Autoencoders: Do SAEs Beat Random Baselines?
papers.research_question: Do Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) learn meaningful feature decompositions of neural network activations, or can their performance be matched by random baselines?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) fail to reliably decompose models' internal mechanisms, as they recover very few ground-truth features in synthetic experiments and are matched in performance by simple random baselines on real model activations.
papers.conclusion: Current SAE evaluation practices are insufficient, and SAEs in their present state do not reliably learn meaningful feature decompositions. The proposed random baselines serve as simple sanity checks for future work.
papers.key_findings:
In synthetic experiments with known ground-truth features, SAEs recover only 9% of true features despite achieving 71% explained variance, showing a disconnect between reconstruction and feature recovery.
Three random baselines (Frozen Decoder, Soft-Frozen Decoder, Frozen Encoder) match fully-trained SAEs across key evaluation metrics: interpretability (0.87 vs 0.90), sparse probing (0.69 vs 0.72), and causal editing (0.73 vs 0.72).
In the synthetic variable probability setting, SAEs recover only the highest-frequency ground-truth features, leaving over 90% of the feature dictionary unmatched.
The reconstruction objective is a poor proxy for meaningful decomposition, as SAEs can achieve strong reconstruction without aligning with true features.
The competitive performance of frozen baselines suggests SAEs may operate in a 'lazy training' regime, achieving most gains through minimal adjustments to randomly initialized components.
papers.limitation:
The synthetic experiment assumes independent feature activations, omitting correlations that likely exist in real neural networks.
The work focuses on standard SAE architectures and does not evaluate related approaches such as transcoders or crosscoders.
future_direction: Explore objectives that more directly incentivize feature alignment rather than just reconstruction.
Design appropriate randomization baselines for related methods like transcoders and crosscoders.
Incorporate more realistic feature dependencies in synthetic evaluation setups.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising tool for interpreting neural networks by decomposing their activations into sparse sets of human-interpretable features. Recent work has introduced multiple SAE variants and successfully scaled them to frontier models. Despite much excitement, a growing number of negative results in downstream tasks casts doubt on whether SAEs recover meaningful features. To directly investigate this, we perform two complementary evaluations. On a synthetic setup with known ground-truth features, we demonstrate that SAEs recover only $9\%$ of true features despite achieving $71\%$ explained variance, showing that they fail at their core task even when reconstruction is strong. To evaluate SAEs on real activations, we introduce three baselines that constrain SAE feature directions or their activation patterns to random values. Through extensive experiments across multiple SAE architectures, we show that our baselines match fully-trained SAEs in interpretability (0.87 vs 0.90), sparse probing (0.69 vs 0.72), and causal editing (0.73 vs 0.72). Together, these results suggest that SAEs in their current state do not reliably decompose models' internal mechanisms.

papers.title: TPA: Next Token Probability Attribution for Detecting Hallucinations in RAG
papers.research_question: Is the binary conflict between FFNs and RAG the only cause of hallucination? Do contributions from other components like LayerNorm and User Query also drive hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: TPA is a novel framework that mathematically attributes each token's probability to seven distinct sources (Query, RAG Context, Past Token, Self Token, FFN, Final LayerNorm, Initial Embedding) and uses syntax-aware aggregation to detect hallucinations in RAG, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
papers.conclusion: TPA effectively detects RAG hallucinations by attributing token probability to seven sources and using syntax-aware features, outperforming baselines and showing that hallucination signals vary across models, necessitating a learnable approach.
papers.key_findings:
TPA achieves state-of-the-art hallucination detection performance across diverse LLM architectures (Llama2, Llama3, Mistral, Qwen3).
Fine-grained attribution beyond the binary FFN-RAG conflict is necessary for robust detection; previously overlooked sources like LayerNorm are vital.
Syntactic aggregation (by POS tags) captures model-specific grounding logic, enabling the detector to pinpoint anomalies in specific entities.
Hallucination fingerprints vary across model architectures, confirming the need for a learnable approach rather than static heuristics.
The method provides transparent interpretability, automatically uncovering novel mechanistic signatures such as anomalous LayerNorm contributions.
papers.limitation:
Relies on white-box access to model internals, preventing application to closed-source APIs.
The decomposition incurs higher computational overhead than simple scalar probes.
Feature engineering depends on external linguistic tools (POS taggers), which may limit generalization to specialized domains like code generation.
future_direction: Extending TPA to phrase- or span-level attribution for efficiency.
Active mitigation via online monitoring and intervention on risky patterns (e.g., abnormal FFN or LN reliance).
Studying TPA under noisy or adversarial retrieval, where expected source shifts may themselves serve as detection signals.
Extending POS-based aggregation to non-English and specialized domains (code, scientific text) via multilingual spaCy or AST node types.
papers.abstract: Detecting hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation remains a challenge. Prior approaches attribute hallucinations to a binary conflict between internal knowledge stored in FFNs and the retrieved context. However, this perspective is incomplete, failing to account for the impact of other components of the LLM, such as the user query, previously generated tokens, the self token, and the final LayerNorm adjustment. To comprehensively capture the impact of these components on hallucination detection, we propose TPA which mathematically attributes each token's probability to seven distinct sources: Query, RAG Context, Past Token, Self Token, FFN, Final LayerNorm, and Initial Embedding. This attribution quantifies how each source contributes to the generation of the next token. Specifically, we aggregate these attribution scores by Part-of-Speech (POS) tags to quantify the contribution of each model component to the generation of specific linguistic categories within a response. By leveraging these patterns, such as detecting anomalies where Nouns rely heavily on LayerNorm, TPA effectively identifies hallucinated responses. Extensive experiments show that TPA achieves state-of-the-art performance.

papers.title: The Hypocrisy Gap: Quantifying Divergence Between Internal Belief and Chain-of-Thought Explanation via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the divergence between a model's internal belief and its chain-of-thought explanation to detect unfaithful behavior like sycophancy?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Hypocrisy Gap, a mechanistic metric using Sparse Autoencoders to quantify divergence between a model's internal truth alignment and its chain-of-thought explanation, and demonstrates its effectiveness in detecting sycophantic behavior.
papers.conclusion: The Hypocrisy Gap provides a practical white-box diagnostic for unfaithful rationalizations in LLMs, highlighting a concrete latent signature of when models say what they do not believe.
papers.key_findings:
The Hypocrisy Gap achieves AUROC of 0.55–0.73 for detecting sycophantic runs and 0.55–0.74 for hypocritical cases, outperforming a log-probability baseline (0.41–0.50 AUROC).
Sycophantic runs concentrate in a specific quadrant where internal truth scores are high but explanation truth scores are low, indicating unfaithful rationalization.
The method is lightweight, requiring only cached activations, a pretrained SAE encoder, and a sparse linear probe.
Task-specific SAE training and fine-tuning can improve performance but require additional compute and data.
The neutral truth score (T) alone provides modest signal for sycophancy detection, while the explanation score (F) is a poor indicator.
papers.limitation:
Requires access to internal activations and a compatible pretrained SAE, so it does not apply to closed-weight or API-based models.
The learned truth direction may capture template-, model-, or layer-specific correlations rather than a template-invariant representation of factual correctness.
Averaging CoT activations over continuation tokens can blur distinct phases of reasoning; more granular temporal aggregation may yield sharper signals.
Evaluation is limited to a single benchmark and a limited set of models, so generalization to other domains, alternative forms of deception, and multilingual settings remains uncertain.
The metric operationalizes 'internal belief' as alignment with a learned truth direction in representation space and should not be interpreted as an agentic or philosophical notion of belief.
future_direction: More granular temporal aggregation of CoT activations to yield sharper signals.
Generalization to other domains, alternative forms of deception, and multilingual settings.
More rigorous training of task-specific SAEs on more examples to improve performance.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently exhibit unfaithful behavior, producing a final answer that differs significantly from their internal chain of thought (CoT) reasoning in order to appease the user they are conversing with. In order to better detect this behavior, we introduce the Hypocrisy Gap, a mechanistic metric utilizing Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to quantify the divergence between a model's internal reasoning and its final generation. By mathematically comparing an internal truth belief, derived via sparse linear probes, to the final generated trajectory in latent space, we quantify and detect a model's tendency to engage in unfaithful behavior. Experiments on Gemma, Llama, and Qwen models using Anthropic's Sycophancy benchmark show that our method achieves an AUROC of 0.55-0.73 for detecting sycophantic runs and 0.55-0.74 for hypocritical cases where the model internally "knows" the user is wrong, consistently outperforming a decision-aligned log-probability baseline (0.41-0.50 AUROC).

papers.title: Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders for Monosemantic Representation
papers.research_question: How do concept activation distributions differ between Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and their base models, and do SAEs promote more monosemantic representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a distribution-aware concept separability score and shows that Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) reduce polysemanticity and achieve higher concept separability than their dense base models. It also proposes a new intervention method, Attenuation via Posterior Probabilities (APP), which enables effective concept removal with minimal side effects.
papers.conclusion: This work presents the first quantitative analysis of monosemanticity in SAEs compared to dense base models through a distributional lens, introduces a fine-grained concept separability score, and proposes a new intervention method (APP) that achieves effective concept removal with the least possible side effects.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs exhibit lower polysemanticity (neuron overlap) and higher concept separability than their base models across multiple datasets and models.
SAEs enable more precise concept-level interventions than base models, particularly when using partial suppression methods.
The proposed APP intervention method achieves the smallest perplexity increase while remaining highly competitive at concept removal.
Higher-capacity SAEs (e.g., 65k dimensions) yield greater concept separability and more effective interventions than lower-capacity ones.
A strong positive correlation exists between the concept separability score and the precision of partial concept erasure methods.
papers.limitation: APP uses a histogram-based approximation for density estimation to improve computational efficiency, which trades off accuracy and computational cost. Achieving the best possible performance requires significantly higher computational resources.
future_direction: Future work could explore alternative kernel density estimation (KDE) methods to better balance accuracy and efficiency for the APP method.
papers.abstract: A key barrier to interpreting large language models is polysemanticity, where neurons activate for multiple unrelated concepts. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have been proposed to mitigate this issue by transforming dense activations into sparse, more interpretable features. While prior work suggests that SAEs promote monosemanticity, no quantitative comparison has examined how concept activation distributions differ between SAEs and their base models. This paper provides the first systematic evaluation of SAEs against base models through activation distribution lens. We introduce a fine-grained concept separability score based on the Jensen-Shannon distance, which captures how distinctly a neuron's activation distributions vary across concepts. Using two large language models (Gemma-2-2B and DeepSeek-R1) and multiple SAE variants across five datasets (including word-level and sentence-level), we show that SAEs reduce polysemanticity and achieve higher concept separability. To assess practical utility, we evaluate concept-level interventions using two strategies: full neuron masking and partial suppression. We find that, compared to base models, SAEs enable more precise concept-level control when using partial suppression. Building on this, we propose Attenuation via Posterior Probabilities (APP), a new intervention method that uses concept-conditioned activation distributions for targeted suppression. APP achieves the smallest perplexity increase while remaining highly effective at concept removal.

papers.title: Uncovering Cross-Linguistic Disparities in LLMs using Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What are the systematic activation disparities between high-resource and medium-to-low resource languages in multilingual LLMs, and can activation-aware fine-tuning reduce these disparities and improve performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals systematic activation disparities in multilingual LLMs, where medium-to-low resource languages receive significantly lower activations, and demonstrates that activation-aware fine-tuning can reduce these disparities and lead to modest improvements in benchmark performance.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit systematic activation disparities across languages despite embedding similarity, and while fine-tuning reduces activation gaps, its effect on task performance remains limited, highlighting the need for more effective adaptation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Medium-to-low resource languages exhibit up to 26.27% lower activations in early layers compared to high-resource languages, with a persistent gap of 19.89% in deeper layers.
Activation disparities are correlated with performance gaps on multilingual benchmarks (ARC-C, MMLU, HellaSwag).
Activation-aware fine-tuning via LoRA substantially increases activations for medium-to-low resource languages (e.g., 87.69% for Malayalam) while retaining English activations at ~91%.
Fine-tuning leads to modest but consistent improvements in benchmark performance, such as a 1.44-point increase in ARC-C accuracy for Malayalam.
Embedding similarity does not guarantee equitable activation dynamics or performance, challenging the assumption that it indicates equal linguistic understanding.
papers.limitation:
Translation errors from Helsinki-NLP models may introduce bias and misalign activation patterns, particularly for medium-to-low resource languages.
Benchmark performance improvements from fine-tuning are modest, suggesting activation alignment alone is insufficient for full convergence to shared representations.
Findings are based on Gemma-2-2B, and it remains unclear whether similar activation disparities exist across other model architectures.
future_direction: Refining fine-tuning techniques to better translate activation alignment into performance gains.
Extending the analysis to other LLMs and multilingual datasets to further improve language equity in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong cross-linguistic generalization, yet medium to low resource languages underperform on common benchmarks such as ARC-Challenge, MMLU, and HellaSwag. We analyze activation patterns in Gemma-2-2B across all 26 residual layers and 10 languages: Chinese (zh), Russian (ru), Spanish (es), Italian (it), medium to low resource languages including Indonesian (id), Catalan (ca), Marathi (mr), Malayalam (ml), and Hindi (hi), with English (en) as the reference. Using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), we reveal systematic disparities in activation patterns. Medium to low resource languages receive up to 26.27 percent lower activations in early layers, with a persistent gap of 19.89 percent in deeper layers. To address this, we apply activation-aware fine-tuning via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), leading to substantial activation gains, such as 87.69 percent for Malayalam and 86.32 percent for Hindi, while maintaining English retention at approximately 91 percent. After fine-tuning, benchmark results show modest but consistent improvements, highlighting activation alignment as a key factor in enhancing multilingual LLM performance.

papers.title: Which Sparse Autoencoder Features Are Real? Model-X Knockoffs for False Discovery Rate Control
papers.research_question: How can we distinguish real computational patterns from erroneous correlations in sparse autoencoder features? The paper investigates using Model-X knockoffs for false discovery rate control in SAE feature selection.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Model-X knockoffs for selecting sparse autoencoder features with false discovery rate control, revealing that only 25% of highly active SAE features encode genuine task-relevant information.
papers.conclusion: The method provides a rigorous statistical framework for identifying genuine SAE features with FDR control, addressing a critical gap in interpretability research and showing that naive feature analysis approaches are dominated by false positives.
papers.key_findings:
The method selected 129 features at a target FDR q=0.1 from 512 high-activity SAE latents for sentiment classification.
Selected features show a 5.40× separation in knockoff statistics compared to non-selected features.
Only about 25% of the examined latents carry task-relevant signal, while 75% do not.
A classifier using only the selected features achieved 77.4% training accuracy.
Features with negative knockoff statistics exist, indicating misleading patterns that would be selected by naive correlation-based approaches.
papers.limitation:
Feature reduction is necessary for stable covariance estimation (n > p), which may miss rare but important features.
Computational cost scales quadratically in p, becoming expensive for very large feature sets.
The method identifies which features are real but does not explain what those features represent.
The method identifies statistical association, not necessarily causal importance.
future_direction: Explore hierarchical testing strategies, approximate knockoff methods, or alternative covariance estimation techniques to handle p ≫ n settings.
Combine knockoff-based selection with automated interpretation pipelines to provide both statistical validation and conceptual understanding.
Investigate how feature validity varies across layers and tasks, and how selection interacts with different SAE training objectives and architectures.
papers.abstract: Although sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are crucial for identifying interpretable features in neural networks, it is still challenging to distinguish between real computational patterns and erroneous correlations. We introduce Model-X knockoffs to SAE feature selection, using knock-off+ to control the false discovery rate (FDR) with finite-sample guarantees under the standard Model-X assumptions (in our case, via a Gaussian surrogate for the latent distribution). We select 129 features at a target FDR q=0.1 after analyzing 512 high-activity SAE latents for sentiment classification using Pythia-70M. About 25% of the latents under examination carry task-relevant signal, whereas 75% do not, according to the chosen set, which displays a 5.40x separation in knockoff statistics compared to non-selected features. Our method offers a re-producible and principled framework for reliable feature discovery by combining SAEs with multiple-testing-aware inference, advancing the foundations of mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: On the transferability of Sparse Autoencoders for interpreting compressed models
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) trained on uncompressed models be effectively transferred to interpret compressed (pruned) models, and is pruning the original SAE itself a viable alternative to training a new SAE on the pruned model?
papers.core_contribution: SAEs pretrained on uncompressed models can be transferred to pruned models with minimal performance loss, and pruning the original SAE itself achieves performance comparable to training a new SAE on the pruned model, offering a computationally efficient alternative.
papers.conclusion: Retraining SAEs for each compressed model variant may be unnecessary; pruning the pretrained SAE offers a practical and computationally efficient alternative for post-hoc interpretability analysis of compressed models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on the original model can interpret the compressed model with only slight performance degradation compared to SAEs trained on the compressed model.
Pruning a pretrained SAE (e.g., to 25% sparsity) yields performance comparable to training a new SAE on the pruned model, eliminating the need for costly retraining.
The transferability and pruning effectiveness hold across different model architectures (GPT-2 and Gemma-2-2B) and across various interpretability metrics (reconstruction, feature absorption, SCR, TPP, RAVEL).
future_direction: Explore the generalization of these findings to quantized and low-rank compressed models.
Further investigate the role of pruning as an implicit regularizer in interpretability systems.
papers.abstract: Modern LLMs face inference efficiency challenges due to their scale. To address this, many compression methods have been proposed, such as pruning and quantization. However, the effect of compression on a model's interpretability remains elusive. While several model interpretation approaches exist, such as circuit discovery, Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have proven particularly effective in decomposing a model's activation space into its feature basis. In this work, we explore the differences in SAEs for the original and compressed models. We find that SAEs trained on the original model can interpret the compressed model albeit with slight performance degradation compared to the trained SAE on the compressed model. Furthermore, simply pruning the original SAE itself achieves performance comparable to training a new SAE on the pruned model. This finding enables us to mitigate the extensive training costs of SAEs.

papers.title: SAKED: Mitigating Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models via Stability-Aware Knowledge Enhanced Decoding
papers.research_question: How does instability in a model's internal knowledge contribute to hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SAKED, a training-free decoding method that uses a layer-wise Knowledge Stability Score (KSS) to quantify and leverage stable internal knowledge, thereby mitigating hallucinations in LVLMs without additional training.
papers.conclusion: SAKED effectively mitigates hallucinations by dynamically leveraging stable internal knowledge, providing a practical step toward safer and more reliable multimodal generation.
papers.key_findings:
Visual activation drift across attention heads is associated with hallucinations.
Large knowledge fluctuations across model layers correlate with higher hallucination risk.
Substantial distraction in visual focus between neighboring output tokens increases the likelihood of hallucinations.
SAKED achieves state-of-the-art hallucination mitigation performance across multiple models and benchmarks.
SAKED is a plug-and-play method that does not require model fine-tuning.
papers.limitation: In early generation stages with short sequences, the Cross-Token Stability Score (CTSS) has limited impact because temporal dependencies are less pronounced.
future_direction: Investigate more flexible ways to leverage CHSS, CLSS, and CTSS throughout the generation process with adaptive weighting.
Explore using CHSS, CLSS, and CTSS as auxiliary supervision signals during training to encourage models to suppress hallucination-prone behaviors.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) pose significant security and reliability risks in real-world applications. Inspired by the observation that humans are more error-prone when uncertain or hesitant, we investigate how instability in a model 's internal knowledge contributes to LVLM hallucinations. We conduct extensive empirical analyses from three perspectives, namely attention heads, model layers, and decoding tokens, and identify three key hallucination patterns: (i) visual activation drift across attention heads, (ii) pronounced knowledge fluctuations across layers, and (iii) visual focus distraction between neighboring output tokens. Building on these findings, we propose Stability-Aware Knowledge-Enhanced Decoding (SAKED), which introduces a layer-wise Knowledge Stability Score (KSS) to quantify knowledge stability throughout the model. By contrasting the most stability-aware and stability-agnostic layers, SAKED suppresses decoding noise and dynamically leverages the most reliable internal knowledge for faithful token generation. Moreover, SAKED is training-free and can be seamlessly integrated into different architectures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAKED achieves state-of-the-art performance for hallucination mitigation on various models, tasks, and benchmarks.

papers.title: Analyzing Hierarchical Structure in Vision Models with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Do the internal representations of vision models align with the ImageNet hierarchy, and can Sparse Autoencoders reveal this structure? How consistent is this structure across different layers, and can SAE-derived representations quantify the degree to which a model respects taxonomic relationships?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Autoencoders as a tool for analyzing hierarchical structure in vision models, demonstrating that SAEs can reveal how DINOv2 encodes ImageNet taxonomic relationships in its representations, with increasing information in later layers.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are effective for probing hierarchical structure in vision models, revealing that DINOv2 implicitly encodes taxonomic information, with stronger alignment in later layers.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers of DINOv2's class token contain little information, while later layers gain more hierarchical information.
SAEs extract features that align with ImageNet hierarchy, with higher ontological coverage in later layers.
Specific SAE heads capture higher-order concepts such as elasmodranch, whales, woodwind instruments, and warships.
SAE metrics can serve as a surrogate for identifying information in representations without the need for labels.
The model encodes hierarchical concepts increasingly through each processing layer.
papers.limitation:
Limited to a single vision foundation model, DINOv2, and may not generalize to all architectures.
Focus on ImageNet hierarchy, which may not be comprehensive or universally applicable for all visual concepts.
Reliance on SAEs introduces interpretability challenges, such as feature redundancy or artifacts from sparsity constraints.
Hierarchical metrics may not fully capture all nuances of taxonomic representation within vision models.
future_direction: Extend analysis to diverse models and taxonomies, including those from human perception studies.
Use advanced XAI methods, such as causal interventions, to further clarify hierarchical encoding.
Apply SAEs to hierarchical classification and concept-based model editing.
papers.abstract: The ImageNet hierarchy provides a structured taxonomy of object categories, offering a valuable lens through which to analyze the representations learned by deep vision models. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of how vision models encode the ImageNet hierarchy, leveraging Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to probe their internal representations. SAEs have been widely used as an explanation tool for large language models (LLMs), where they enable the discovery of semantically meaningful features. Here, we extend their use to vision models to investigate whether learned representations align with the ontological structure defined by the ImageNet taxonomy. Our results show that SAEs uncover hierarchical relationships in model activations, revealing an implicit encoding of taxonomic structure. We analyze the consistency of these representations across different layers of the popular vision foundation model DINOv2 and provide insights into how deep vision models internalize hierarchical category information by increasing information in the class token through each layer. Our study establishes a framework for systematic hierarchical analysis of vision model representations and highlights the potential of SAEs as a tool for probing semantic structure in deep networks.

papers.title: Hallucination Begins Where Saliency Drops
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between gradient-based saliency and hallucinations in large vision-language models, and how can saliency be used to mitigate hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces LVLMs-Saliency, a gradient-based diagnostic tool for token-level hallucination in LVLMs, and proposes two inference-time methods (SGRS and LocoRE) that use saliency to reduce hallucinations by reinforcing contextual dependencies.
papers.conclusion: The proposed saliency-based framework effectively reduces hallucinations in LVLMs without requiring model retraining, offering an interpretable and robust solution.
papers.key_findings:
Hallucinations occur when prior output tokens show low saliency to the next token, indicating a failure of contextual memory.
The proposed Saliency-Guided Rejection Sampling (SGRS) dynamically filters candidate tokens during decoding by rejecting those with saliency below a context-adaptive threshold.
Local Coherence Reinforcement (LocoRE) strengthens attention from the current token to its most recent outputs, counteracting the 'forgetting' behavior.
The combined SGRS and LocoRE framework significantly reduces hallucinations across multiple LVLMs on various benchmarks.
The method is training-free and operates at inference time, making it a plug-and-play solution.
papers.limitation:
The full framework (SGRS+LocoRE) incurs higher latency due to the backward pass required for saliency computation.
There are failure cases where hallucinated tokens exhibit high saliency, particularly when the model is overconfident or the context is ambiguous.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have examined attention dynamics in large vision-language models (LVLMs) to detect hallucinations. However, existing approaches remain limited in reliably distinguishing hallucinated from factually grounded outputs, as they rely solely on forward-pass attention patterns and neglect gradient-based signals that reveal how token influence propagates through the network. To bridge this gap, we introduce LVLMs-Saliency, a gradient-aware diagnostic framework that quantifies the visual grounding strength of each output token by fusing attention weights with their input gradients. Our analysis uncovers a decisive pattern: hallucinations frequently arise when preceding output tokens exhibit low saliency toward the prediction of the next token, signaling a breakdown in contextual memory retention. Leveraging this insight, we propose a dual-mechanism inference-time framework to mitigate hallucinations: (1) Saliency-Guided Rejection Sampling (SGRS), which dynamically filters candidate tokens during autoregressive decoding by rejecting those whose saliency falls below a context-adaptive threshold, thereby preventing coherence-breaking tokens from entering the output sequence; and (2) Local Coherence Reinforcement (LocoRE), a lightweight, plug-and-play module that strengthens attention from the current token to its most recent predecessors, actively counteracting the contextual forgetting behavior identified by LVLMs-Saliency. Extensive experiments across multiple LVLMs demonstrate that our method significantly reduces hallucination rates while preserving fluency and task performance, offering a robust and interpretable solution for enhancing model reliability. Code is available at: https://github.com/zhangbaijin/LVLMs-Saliency

papers.title: Teach Old SAEs New Domain Tricks with Boosting
papers.research_question: How can we address feature blindness in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for domain-specific interpretability without requiring complete retraining?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAE Boost, a residual learning approach that trains a secondary SAE to model the reconstruction error of a pretrained SAE on domain-specific texts, enabling selective enhancement of interpretability for specialized domains without full retraining.
papers.conclusion: SAE Boost addresses feature blindness in SAEs, enabling selective domain enhancement without modifying the base model, and represents an important step forward in targeted mechanistic interpretability of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
SAE Boost significantly improves explained variance and LLM cross-entropy on domain-specific texts compared to a pretrained SAE alone.
The method maintains general domain performance with minimal degradation, confirming it learns complementary features.
SAE Boost captures domain-specific features that general-purpose SAEs miss, as shown by interpretability analysis and lower cosine similarity to base features.
The approach is modular, allowing multiple domain-specific residual SAEs to be applied simultaneously without compromising performance.
SAE Boost outperforms alternative domain adaptation methods like Extended SAE and SAE Stitching in balancing domain performance, general performance, and sparsity.
papers.limitation:
Undertraining the residual SAE (e.g., on fewer than 100M tokens) can degrade general domain performance by up to 31% in explained variance.
Early stopping based solely on domain-specific metrics may lead to suboptimal feature quality.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders have emerged as powerful tools for interpreting the internal representations of Large Language Models, yet they often fail to capture domain-specific features not prevalent in their training corpora. This paper introduces a residual learning approach that addresses this feature blindness without requiring complete retraining. We propose training a secondary SAE specifically to model the reconstruction error of a pretrained SAE on domain-specific texts, effectively capturing features missed by the primary model. By summing the outputs of both models during inference, we demonstrate significant improvements in both LLM cross-entropy and explained variance metrics across multiple specialized domains. Our experiments show that this method efficiently incorporates new domain knowledge into existing SAEs while maintaining their performance on general tasks. This approach enables researchers to selectively enhance SAE interpretability for specific domains of interest, opening new possibilities for targeted mechanistic interpretability of LLMs.

papers.title: Feature Hedging: Correlated Features Break Narrow Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Why do sparse autoencoders (SAEs) underperform relative to other techniques, and can we fix the problems? Specifically, the paper investigates the problem of 'feature hedging' in narrow SAEs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies 'feature hedging' as a fundamental problem in narrow sparse autoencoders (SAEs) where correlated features are merged, degrading monosemanticity, and proposes an improved variant called balance matryoshka SAEs to mitigate this issue.
papers.conclusion: Feature hedging is a core theoretical problem in SAEs that contributes to their underperformance, and the proposed balance matryoshka SAE architecture is a step towards addressing both hedging and absorption, though both problems remain.
papers.key_findings:
Feature hedging occurs when an SAE is too narrow to represent all underlying features and features are correlated, causing the SAE to merge components of correlated features into single latents.
Hedging is caused by the reconstruction (MSE) loss and becomes more severe the narrower the SAE.
In LLM SAEs, hedging is likely the norm due to the high number of correlated features and the SAE being narrower than the number of underlying features.
Balance matryoshka SAEs, which tune the relative loss coefficients between inner and outer levels, can improve performance by better balancing the competing forces of hedging and absorption.
SAE width is not a neutral hyperparameter: narrower SAEs suffer more from hedging, while wider SAEs suffer more from absorption.
papers.limitation: Only test hedging in SAEs up to 65k latents on LLMs with 2b parameters due to compute constraints.
future_direction: Improving balance matryoshka SAEs by learning different balancing coefficients per latent rather than a single coefficient for all latents.
papers.abstract: It is assumed that sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose polysemantic activations into interpretable linear directions, as long as the activations are composed of sparse linear combinations of underlying features. However, we find that if an SAE is more narrow than the number of underlying "true features" on which it is trained, and there is correlation between features, the SAE will merge components of correlated features together, thus destroying monosemanticity. In LLM SAEs, these two conditions are almost certainly true. This phenomenon, which we call feature hedging, is caused by SAE reconstruction loss, and is more severe the narrower the SAE. In this work, we introduce the problem of feature hedging and study it both theoretically in toy models and empirically in SAEs trained on LLMs. We suspect that feature hedging may be one of the core reasons that SAEs consistently underperform supervised baselines. Finally, we use our understanding of feature hedging to propose an improved variant of matryoshka SAEs. Importantly, our work shows that SAE width is not a neutral hyperparameter: narrower SAEs suffer more from hedging than wider SAEs.

papers.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 3.1, Knowledge Storage and Extraction
papers.research_question: How do language models memorize knowledge during training, and extract it later to answer questions or perform logical reasoning during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that knowledge augmentation (e.g., paraphrasing, sentence shuffling) in pretraining data is crucial for reliable knowledge extraction via instruction fine-tuning, and introduces linear probing techniques to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes with practical recommendations for LLM pretraining: data rewriting (augmentation) is important, and including instruction-like data in pretraining is beneficial.
papers.key_findings:
Mixed training (pretraining on both biographies and QA data) enables knowledge extraction, but the model learns in an abnormal way (first from QA then correlates with BIO).
Without knowledge augmentation in pretraining, instruction fine-tuning fails to extract knowledge (0% accuracy).
Knowledge augmentation (e.g., paraphrasing, sentence shuffling, translations) during pretraining enables knowledge extraction after fine-tuning.
Linear probing shows that knowledge augmentation causes knowledge to be linearly encoded in the hidden embeddings of entity names, whereas without augmentation it is distributed across tokens.
Including celebrity data (with augmentation) in pretraining improves knowledge extraction for minority data (without augmentation).
future_direction: Studying logical reasoning and knowledge manipulation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can store a vast amount of world knowledge, often extractable via question-answering (e.g., "What is Abraham Lincoln's birthday?"). However, do they answer such questions based on exposure to similar questions during training (i.e., cheating), or by genuinely learning to extract knowledge from sources like Wikipedia? In this paper, we investigate this issue using a controlled biography dataset. We find a strong correlation between the model's ability to extract knowledge and various diversity measures of the training data. $\textbf{Essentially}$, for knowledge to be reliably extracted, it must be sufficiently augmented (e.g., through paraphrasing, sentence shuffling, translations) $\textit{during pretraining}$. Without such augmentation, knowledge may be memorized but not extractable, leading to 0% accuracy, regardless of subsequent instruction fine-tuning. To understand why this occurs, we employ (nearly) linear probing to demonstrate a strong connection between the observed correlation and how the model internally encodes knowledge -- whether it is linearly encoded in the hidden embeddings of entity names or distributed across other token embeddings in the training text. This paper provides $\textbf{several key recommendations for LLM pretraining in the industry}$: (1) rewrite the pretraining data -- using small, auxiliary models -- to provide knowledge augmentation, and (2) incorporate more instruction-finetuning data into the pretraining stage before it becomes too late.

papers.title: Revis: Sparse Latent Steering to Mitigate Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models be mitigated by reactivating suppressed visual information through sparse latent steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REVIS, a training-free framework that uses orthogonal projection to decouple visual information from language priors in the latent space and performs sparse intervention at an optimal layer to mitigate object hallucination in LVLMs.
papers.conclusion: REVIS effectively mitigates object hallucination in LVLMs by reactivating visual information via sparse latent steering, without compromising general reasoning capabilities or inference efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
REVIS reduces object hallucination rates by approximately 19% compared to state-of-the-art baselines while preserving general reasoning capabilities.
Orthogonal projection is necessary to decouple visual information from entangled language priors, preventing model collapse that occurs with naive steering vectors.
Sparse intervention at a single, optimally selected layer is sufficient and more efficient than dense multi-layer intervention.
The method maintains inference efficiency, adding negligible latency compared to contrastive decoding methods that require multiple forward passes.
REVIS generalizes effectively across diverse LVLM architectures (Qwen, LLaVA, InternVL series).
papers.limitation:
REVIS relies on the base model's representations, limiting its ability to rectify absolute perceptual blindness.
The evaluation focuses on object hallucination and does not cover other types of hallucinations (e.g., attribute, relation).
future_direction: Extending the method to other types of hallucinations (attribute, relation).
Exploring its application in more complex multimodal tasks.
papers.abstract: Despite the advanced capabilities of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), they frequently suffer from object hallucination. One reason is that visual features and pretrained textual representations often become intertwined in the deeper network layers. To address this, we propose REVIS, a training-free framework designed to explicitly re-activate this suppressed visual information. Rooted in latent space geometry, REVIS extracts the pure visual information vector via orthogonal projection and employs a calibrated strategy to perform sparse intervention only at the precise depth where suppression occurs. This surgical approach effectively restores visual information with minimal computational cost. Empirical evaluations on standard benchmarks demonstrate that REVIS reduces object hallucination rates by approximately 19% compared to state-of-the-art baselines, while preserving general reasoning capabilities.

papers.title: Don't Forget It! Conditional Sparse Autoencoder Clamping Works for Unlearning
papers.research_question: How can Sparse Autoencoders be used to unlearn harmful knowledge in large language models while retaining safe knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a conditional SAE-based clamping method for unlearning that improves retention of safe information compared to prior SAE methods and performs comparably to RMU with better interpretability.
papers.conclusion: SAE-based unlearning outperforms prior SAE approaches on retention and performs comparably with RMU on forgetting harmful information while retaining safe information, with fewer hyperparameters and better interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal Clamp achieves the lowest WMDP-bio accuracy (0.2718) and highest alignment score (0.8226), indicating effective unlearning with some impact on general knowledge.
Clamp Prime improves forgetting performance (WMDP-bio accuracy drops to 0.2985) but slightly reduces general knowledge retention compared to RMU.
Adversarial evaluation using Concurrent Greedy Search shows that unlearned models resist suffix attacks, continuing to output gibberish.
The method requires fewer hyperparameter choices than RMU while maintaining interpretability.
SAE-based unlearning is shown to be viable, with conditional steering reducing side effects on safe information.
papers.limitation:
Training sparse autoencoders and labeling the latents is slow and expensive, limiting practicality to models with pre-existing SAEs.
Steering models with sparse autoencoders requires closed weights, as attackers can remove steering hooks if they have access to the weights.
Using Wikitext as the retain set for RMU may cause bias, potentially inflating the method's score on biology-related subjects in evaluation.
future_direction: Investigating which SAE layers allow for the best unlearning.
Exploring the impact of latent space dimensionality (i.e., using SAEs with larger hidden activation shapes).
Training interpretable parameters that edit the SAE latent vector to allow for fully interpretable fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Recent developments in Large Language Model (LLM) capabilities have brought great potential but also posed new risks. For example, LLMs with knowledge of bioweapons, advanced chemistry, or cyberattacks could cause violence if placed in the wrong hands or during malfunctions. Because of their nature as near-black boxes, intuitive interpretation of LLM internals remains an open research question, preventing developers from easily controlling model behavior and capabilities. The use of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) has recently emerged as a potential method of unraveling representations of concepts in LLMs internals, and has allowed developers to steer model outputs by directly modifying the hidden activations. In this paper, we use SAEs to identify unwanted concepts from the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy (WMDP) dataset within gemma-2-2b internals and use feature steering to reduce the model's ability to answer harmful questions while retaining its performance on harmless queries. Our results bring back optimism to the viability of SAE-based explicit knowledge unlearning techniques.

papers.title: Investigating task-specific prompts and sparse autoencoders for activation monitoring
papers.research_question: How do prompted probing and SAE-based probing compare for activation monitoring in language models, and under what constraints (e.g., data availability, compute) are they most effective?
papers.core_contribution: Prompted probing is a data-efficient and effective method for activation monitoring, especially in low-data regimes. SAE-based probing can be effective when inference-time compute is limited, but prompted probing is recommended when inference-time compute is available.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends prompted probing when inference-time compute is available due to its data efficiency and generalization. If inference-time compute is limited, SAE-based probing is a good alternative. Straightforward activation probing is reasonable when both inference-time and train-time compute are limited.
papers.key_findings:
Prompted last token probing is the most data-efficient technique and performs well in low-data regimes.
Prompting is important: prompted last token probe outperforms naive last token probe, especially in low-data regimes.
In high-data regimes, all probing techniques (prompted probing, SAE probing, raw last token probing) can outperform zero-shot model output.
SAE max-pooled probing generalizes poorly out-of-distribution compared to prompted probing in some cases.
For sentiment classification, last token probes perform best, and max-pooling across tokens degrades performance.
papers.limitation:
The work does not compare the methods to fine-tuning the model, which is often the method of choice when labeled training data is available.
Estimates of zero-shot monitoring performance are likely pessimistic due to lack of prompt engineering and not using reasoning models or chain-of-thought.
Few-shot prompting did not improve performance in the studied settings, possibly due to context length limitations or the model's inability to extract useful signal.
future_direction: Exploring unsupervised approaches like LAT Scans for monitoring when labeled data is unavailable.
Investigating the mechanisms underlying prompted probing and whether prompted and un-prompted probing rely on shared representations.
More research into model organisms of emergent deceptive monitors to understand collusion risks.
papers.abstract: Language models can behave in unexpected and unsafe ways, and so it is valuable to monitor their outputs. Internal activations of language models encode additional information that could be useful for this. The baseline approach for activation monitoring is some variation of linear probing on a particular layer: starting from a labeled dataset, train a logistic regression classifier on that layer's activations. Recent work has proposed several approaches which may improve on naive linear probing, by leveraging additional computation. One class of techniques, which we call "prompted probing," leverages test time computation to improve monitoring by (1) prompting the model with a description of the monitoring task, and (2) applying a learned linear probe to resulting activations. Another class of techniques uses computation at train time: training sparse autoencoders offline to identify an interpretable basis for the activations, and e.g. max-pooling activations across tokens using that basis before applying a linear probe. However, one can also prompt the model with a description of the monitoring task and use its output directly. We develop and test novel refinements of these methods and compare them against each other. We find asking the model zero-shot is a reasonable baseline when inference-time compute is not limited; however, activation probing methods can substantially outperform this baseline given sufficient training data. Specifically, we recommend prompted probing when inference-time compute is available, due to its superior data efficiency and good generalization performance. Alternatively, if inference-time compute is limited, we find SAE-based probing methods outperform raw activation probing.

papers.title: Seeing Clearly by Layer Two: Enhancing Attention Heads to Alleviate Hallucination in LVLMs
papers.research_question: How does the pattern of attention sinks in image tokens relate to hallucinations in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), and can enhancing attention heads in shallow layers alleviate hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Enhancing Attention Heads (EAH), a training-free, plug-and-play method that reduces hallucinations in multimodal large language models by identifying and broadcasting the attention map of the head with the densest vision sink in shallow layers.
papers.conclusion: EAH is an effective, training-free, and plug-and-play method for alleviating hallucinations in MLLMs by enhancing attention heads in shallow layers, as validated by extensive benchmark tests and generalization experiments.
papers.key_findings:
Hallucinations in MLLMs are linked to sparse attention sinks in image tokens; denser vision sinks in shallow layers correlate with fewer hallucinations.
The proposed EAH method, which broadcasts the attention map of the head with the densest vision sink to other heads in shallow layers, effectively reduces hallucinations across multiple models and benchmarks.
EAH improves performance on general vision-language tasks without additional computation, demonstrating its plug-and-play convenience and generalization ability.
The method also shows consistent gains in large language models (LLMs) on tasks like GSM8K and TruthfulQA, indicating broader applicability.
Ablation studies confirm that the optimal intervention occurs at layer 2 with a specific threshold, and broadcasting to all heads in the layer yields the best results.
papers.limitation: EAH exhibits about a 4 percentage point lower recall compared to other methods at the same average output length.
future_direction: Improved alignment of projectors and advanced training methods, such as reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), are needed for more fundamental resolution of hallucination issues.
papers.abstract: The hallucination problem in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remains a common issue. Although image tokens occupy a majority of the input sequence of MLLMs, there is limited research to explore the relationship between image tokens and hallucinations. In this paper, we analyze the distribution of attention scores for image tokens across each layer and head of the model, revealing an intriguing and common phenomenon: most hallucinations are closely linked to the pattern of attention sinks in the self-attention matrix of image tokens, where shallow layers exhibit dense attention sinks and deeper layers show sparse attention sinks. We further analyze the attention heads of different layers and find that heads with high-density attention sink in the image part play a positive role in alleviating hallucinations. In this paper, we propose a training-free method named \textcolor{red}{\textbf{E}}nhancing \textcolor{red}{\textbf{A}}ttention \textcolor{red}{\textbf{H}}eads (EAH), an approach designed to enhance the convergence of image tokens attention sinks in the shallow layers. EAH identifies the attention head that shows the vision sink in a shallow layer and extracts its attention matrix. This attention map is then broadcast to other heads in the layer, thereby strengthening the layer to pay more attention to the image itself. With extensive experiments, EAH shows significant hallucination-mitigating performance on different MLLMs and metrics, proving its effectiveness and generality.

papers.title: Open Roles In Interpretability Scaling Laws for Dictionary Learning Update on how we train SAEs How Strongly do Dictionary Learning Features Influence Model Behavior? Interpretability Architectures Project Caloric and the Utility of Incorrect Theories Open Problem: Attribution Dictionary Learning Isolating Circuits Paths of Different Lengths
papers.core_contribution: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling laws for dictionary learning show that loss decreases approximately as a power law with compute, with optimal allocations of training steps and features scaling as power laws.
An improved SAE training setup with modified loss function and initialization reduces loss and allows scaling to millions of features without issues.
Ablating dictionary learning features causes significantly more loss increase than random perturbations, indicating that features are high-leverage for model behavior.
Feature ablations have a larger effect than feature doublings, suggesting that feature influence may saturate at higher activations.
The impact of feature ablations is more pronounced for residual stream features compared to MLP features, hinting at different functional roles.
papers.limitation:
The relationship between SAE loss and qualitative usefulness of SAE features is imperfect and may break down at sufficient scale.
The SAE training initialization may need improvement and could cause issues for large feature counts.
The results on feature influence are preliminary and require further investigation.
future_direction: Exploring interpretable model architectures
Investigating attribution dictionary learning
Improving SAE training methods such as initialization and post-training
papers.abstract: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior. The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.

papers.title: Incorporating Hierarchical Semantics in Sparse Autoencoder Architectures
papers.research_question: Does incorporating hierarchical structure into sparse autoencoder architectures improve the reconstruction-interpretability frontier? Specifically, does it improve reconstruction, maintain or improve interpretability, and learn hierarchical semantics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Hierarchical Sparse Autoencoder (H-SAE) architecture that explicitly models semantic hierarchy, improving reconstruction performance and interpretability while being computationally efficient.
papers.conclusion: Incorporating hierarchical structure into sparse autoencoder architectures improves the reconstruction-interpretability frontier, leading to better reconstruction, maintained or improved interpretability, and learned hierarchical semantics.
papers.key_findings:
H-SAEs have better reconstruction performance than standard SAEs as measured by explained variance and downstream CE loss.
H-SAEs maintain or improve interpretability, showing less feature absorption and fewer redundant features across languages.
The H-SAE architecture learns hierarchical semantics, with high-level features capturing general concepts and low-level features capturing specific instances.
The hierarchical structure provides significant computational efficiency gains, allowing scaling to larger effective dictionary sizes with minimal overhead.
The architecture successfully translates theoretical insights about hierarchical concept geometry into a practical mixture-of-experts type model.
papers.limitation: Results are still imperfect, with some hard-to-interpret features and far from perfect reconstruction.
future_direction: Explore other reconstruction objectives beyond Euclidean distance.
Incorporate insights from causal representation learning into LLM interpretability.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning (and, in particular, sparse autoencoders) attempts to learn a set of human-understandable concepts that can explain variation on an abstract space. A basic limitation of this approach is that it neither exploits nor represents the semantic relationships between the learned concepts. In this paper, we introduce a modified SAE architecture that explicitly models a semantic hierarchy of concepts. Application of this architecture to the internal representations of large language models shows both that semantic hierarchy can be learned, and that doing so improves both reconstruction and interpretability. Additionally, the architecture leads to significant improvements in computational efficiency.

papers.title: Measuring Sparse Autoencoder Feature Sensitivity
papers.research_question: How can we measure the sensitivity of Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features, i.e., how reliably they activate on texts similar to their activating examples?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a scalable, explanation-free method to evaluate SAE feature sensitivity, demonstrating that sensitivity is a novel dimension of feature quality and that many interpretable features have poor sensitivity, with sensitivity declining as SAE width increases.
papers.conclusion: The work establishes feature sensitivity as a crucial dimension for evaluating both individual SAE features and SAE architectures, emphasizing the need for better sensitivity in scaled SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Developed a generation-based method to evaluate SAE feature sensitivity without needing natural language descriptions.
Sensitivity measures a new aspect of feature quality, weakly correlated with existing metrics like interpretability and frequency.
Many interpretable SAE features have poor sensitivity, indicating they do not reliably activate on similar inputs.
Human evaluation confirms that generated text genuinely resembles activating examples when features fail to activate.
Average feature sensitivity declines with increasing SAE width across 7 SAE variants, highlighting a challenge in SAE scaling.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation limited to frequently occurring features, biasing analysis toward common features and missing rare features.
Filtering for features that remain active on truncated text may bias toward simpler features.
Does not incorporate activation magnitude into the sensitivity evaluation.
future_direction: Scale up evaluation to study less frequent features and use longer text snippets.
Incorporate activation strength into studies of SAE features.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features have become essential tools for mechanistic interpretability research.
