Enhancing feature transferability across diverse scenarios
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) systems suffer from the models' unstable ability to generate valid and factual content, resulting in hallucination generation. Current hallucination detection methods heavily rely on out-of-model information sources, such as RAG to assist the detection, thus bringing heavy additional latency. Recently, internal states of LLMs' inference have been widely used in numerous research works, such as prompt injection detection, etc. Considering the interpretability of LLM internal states and the fact that they do not require external information sources, we introduce such states into LLM hallucination detection. In this paper, we systematically analyze different internal states' revealing features during inference forward and comprehensively evaluate their ability in hallucination detection. Specifically, we cut the forward process of a large language model into three stages: understanding, query, generation, and extracting the internal state from these stages. By analyzing these states, we provide a deep understanding of why the hallucinated content is generated and what happened in the internal state of the models. Then, we introduce these internal states into hallucination detection and conduct comprehensive experiments to discuss the advantages and limitations.

papers.title: Decomposing The Dark Matter of Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the structure of SAE error (dark matter)? Can SAE error be predicted from activations? How do the linearly predictable and nonlinearly predictable components differ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that SAE error (dark matter) is largely linearly predictable from model activations, and that the nonlinear component is qualitatively different, containing fewer not-yet-learned features and being harder to learn.
papers.conclusion: The fact that SAE error can be predicted and analyzed is surprising, indicating SAE errors are worthy of analysis. The presence of constant nonlinear error at fixed sparsity suggests scaling SAEs may not be the only way to explain more of model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
SAE error norms and vectors can be linearly predicted from activations with high accuracy (R2 between 70-95% for norms, 15-72% for vectors).
The scaling behavior of SAE error norms is predictable across different SAE sizes; larger SAEs struggle to reconstruct the same contexts as smaller SAEs.
The nonlinear component of SAE error contains fewer not-yet-learned features, is harder to learn SAEs for, and contributes proportionally to cross entropy loss.
Inference time gradient pursuit reduces total FVU by 3-5% but leaves nonlinear error mostly unchanged.
Linear transformations from earlier layer SAE outputs can reduce nonlinear error and total SAE error.
future_direction: Explore alternative penalties besides sparsity or new ways to learn better dictionaries.
Incorporate low-rank dense side channels in SAE architecture.
Use small-scale trials to forecast SAE scaling behavior.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a promising technique for decomposing language model activations into interpretable linear features. However, current SAEs fall short of completely explaining model performance, resulting in "dark matter": unexplained variance in activations. This work investigates dark matter as an object of study in its own right. Surprisingly, we find that much of SAE dark matter -- about half of the error vector itself and >90% of its norm -- can be linearly predicted from the initial activation vector. Additionally, we find that the scaling behavior of SAE error norms at a per token level is remarkably predictable: larger SAEs mostly struggle to reconstruct the same contexts as smaller SAEs. We build on the linear representation hypothesis to propose models of activations that might lead to these observations. These insights imply that the part of the SAE error vector that cannot be linearly predicted ("nonlinear" error) might be fundamentally different from the linearly predictable component. To validate this hypothesis, we empirically analyze nonlinear SAE error and show that 1) it contains fewer not yet learned features, 2) SAEs trained on it are quantitatively worse, and 3) it is responsible for a proportional amount of the downstream increase in cross entropy loss when SAE activations are inserted into the model. Finally, we examine two methods to reduce nonlinear SAE error: inference time gradient pursuit, which leads to a very slight decrease in nonlinear error, and linear transformations from earlier layer SAE outputs, which leads to a larger reduction.

papers.title: Compute Optimal Inference and Provable Amortisation Gap in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the amortisation gap in sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and can more sophisticated sparse inference methods outperform traditional SAE encoders?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that sparse autoencoder (SAE) encoders are inherently insufficient for accurate sparse inference due to an amortisation gap, and demonstrates empirically that more expressive encoders (like MLPs) and sparse coding methods can outperform SAEs, leading to more interpretable features in large language models.
papers.conclusion: More sophisticated sparse inference methods, such as MLPs and sparse coding, can outperform traditional SAE encoders, reducing the amortisation gap and improving interpretability, which opens new avenues for understanding neural network representations.
papers.key_findings:
SAE encoders have a provable amortisation gap, making them suboptimal for sparse inference even in solvable cases.
Multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and sparse coding consistently outperform SAEs in recovering sparse codes, with sparse coding achieving the highest performance.
The performance advantage of more sophisticated methods is more pronounced in regimes where compressed sensing theory predicts recoverability.
These findings generalize to real-world applications, as shown by training on GPT-2 activations where MLPs yield more interpretable features than SAEs.
The amortisation gap can be reduced with increased compute, with MLPs surpassing SAE performance after a consistent computational threshold.
papers.limitation: The theoretical result on SAE suboptimality is proven for a specific setting (linear-nonlinear encoder, sparse signals in union of subspaces) and may not cover all practical SAE implementations.
future_direction: Pitting optimised sparse coding approaches (e.g., Least Angle Regression, Orthogonal Matching Pursuit) against optimised SAE architectures.
Further exploration of top-k sparse coding with proper hyperparameter tuning to achieve Pareto improvements.
Scaling the methods to larger models and more complex datasets.
papers.abstract: A recent line of work has shown promise in using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to uncover interpretable features in neural network representations. However, the simple linear-nonlinear encoding mechanism in SAEs limits their ability to perform accurate sparse inference. Using compressed sensing theory, we prove that an SAE encoder is inherently insufficient for accurate sparse inference, even in solvable cases. We then decouple encoding and decoding processes to empirically explore conditions where more sophisticated sparse inference methods outperform traditional SAE encoders. Our results reveal substantial performance gains with minimal compute increases in correct inference of sparse codes. We demonstrate this generalises to SAEs applied to large language models, where more expressive encoders achieve greater interpretability. This work opens new avenues for understanding neural network representations and analysing large language model activations.

papers.title: Nullu: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models via HalluSpace Projection
papers.research_question: How can object hallucinations in large vision-language models be mitigated by editing model weights based on a low-rank unsafe subspace (HalluSpace)?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Nullu, a weight-editing method that projects model weights to the null space of a low-rank HalluSpace (identified via SVD on feature differences) to reduce object hallucinations without extra inference cost.
papers.conclusion: Nullu is an effective and efficient method for mitigating object hallucinations in LVLMs by editing model weights via HalluSpace projection, and it preserves or enhances general model capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Nullu effectively reduces object hallucinations (lower CHAIR scores) across multiple LVLMs (LLaVA-1.5, MiniGPT-4, mPLUG-Owl2).
The HalluSpace is low-rank and appears to encode LLM priors that contribute to hallucinations, so null space projection reduces these priors.
Nullu requires no extra inference cost and outperforms existing post-hoc methods in both hallucination reduction and inference speed.
The method also maintains or improves general model performance on benchmarks like MME and LLaVA-Bench.
A theoretical connection is drawn between Nullu and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), both aiming to reduce feature differences that lead to hallucinations.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that large vision-language models (LVLMs) often suffer from the issue of object hallucinations (OH). To mitigate this issue, we introduce an efficient method that edits the model weights based on an unsafe subspace, which we call HalluSpace in this paper. With truthful and hallucinated text prompts accompanying the visual content as inputs, the HalluSpace can be identified by extracting the hallucinated embedding features and removing the truthful representations in LVLMs. By orthogonalizing the model weights, input features will be projected into the Null space of the HalluSpace to reduce OH, based on which we name our method Nullu. We reveal that HalluSpaces generally contain prior information in the large language models (LLMs) applied to build LVLMs, which have been shown as essential causes of OH in previous studies. Therefore, null space projection suppresses the LLMs' priors to filter out the hallucinated features, resulting in contextually accurate outputs. Experiments show that our method can effectively mitigate OH across different LVLM families without extra inference costs and also show strong performance in general LVLM benchmarks. Code is released at https://github.com/Ziwei-Zheng/Nullu.

papers.title: Exposing Hallucinations To Suppress Them: VLMs Representation Editing With Generative Anchors
papers.research_question: Can we design a training-free, self-supervised method to mitigate hallucinations in multimodal large language models without sacrificing informativeness?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training-free, self-supervised method for hallucination mitigation in MLLMs by using dual visual anchors (original image and a reconstructed image from a text-to-image model) to edit decoder hidden states, pulling representations toward faithful semantics and pushing them away from hallucination directions.
papers.conclusion: The proposed training-free, self-supervised method effectively mitigates hallucinations in MLLMs without sacrificing informativeness, shows strong generalization across architectures, and serves as a practical plug-and-play module for building more faithful and reliable models.
papers.key_findings:
The method significantly reduces hallucinations at object, attribute, and relation levels while largely preserving recall and caption richness.
It demonstrates strong cross-architecture generalization across different MLLM models (e.g., LLaVA, Cambrian, InstructBLIP).
When applied to hallucination-free captions, the method introduces almost no side effects, showing robustness and plug-and-play applicability.
The dual-supervision editing mechanism (positive anchor from original image, negative anchor from reconstructed image) achieves an effective trade-off between faithfulness and informativeness.
The hallucination amplification mechanism using a text-to-image model effectively exposes implicit hallucinations, making them detectable for correction.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on the fidelity of the text-to-image (T2I) model, which may introduce noise, especially for fine-grained attributes like color.
There is an inherent trade-off between hallucination mitigation and preserving informativeness/recall.
Layer selection for latent editing is fixed (e.g., third layer) and not adaptive to input characteristics.
future_direction: Explore adaptive strategies for layer selection based on input characteristics or model states.
Integrate stronger generative backbones or develop selective filtering strategies to reduce noise from imperfect T2I reconstructions.
Investigate more principled ways to balance the trade-off, such as adaptive weighting schemes or context-aware editing strategies.
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable success across diverse vision-language tasks, yet they remain highly susceptible to hallucinations, producing content that is fluent but inconsistent with visual evidence. Such hallucinations, spanning objects, attributes, and relations, persist even in larger models, while existing mitigation approaches often require additional finetuning, handcrafted priors, or trade-offs that compromise informativeness and scalability. To address this limitation, we propose a training-free, self-supervised method for hallucination mitigation. Our approach introduces a novel hallucination amplification mechanism: a caption is projected into the visual space via a text-to-image model to reveal implicit hallucination signals, serving as a negative anchor, while the original image provides a positive anchor. Leveraging these dual anchors, we edit decoder hidden states by pulling representations toward faithful semantics and pushing them away from hallucination directions. This correction requires no human priors or additional training costs, ensuring both effectiveness and efficiency. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks show that our method significantly reduces hallucinations at the object, attribute, and relation levels while largely preserving recall and caption richness, e.g., achieving a hallucination reduction by over 5% using LLaVA-v1.5-7B on CHAIR. Furthermore, results on diverse architectures, including LLaVA-NEXT-7B, Cambrian-8B, and InstructBLIP-7B, validate strong cross-architecture generalization. More importantly, when applied to hallucination-free captions, our method introduces almost no side effects, underscoring its robustness and practical plug-and-play applicability. The implementation will be publicly available.

papers.title: Temporal Sparse Autoencoders: Leveraging the Sequential Nature of Language for Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we incorporate temporal consistency into sparse autoencoders to better recover high-level semantic features in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Temporal Sparse Autoencoders (T-SAEs) that incorporate a temporal contrastive loss to encourage consistent activations of high-level features over adjacent tokens, leading to better disentanglement of semantic and syntactic features in language models.
papers.conclusion: Temporal SAEs leverage the sequential nature of language to better extract semantic features, offering a new pathway for unsupervised interpretability in language models.
papers.key_findings:
T-SAEs recover smoother, more coherent semantic concepts without sacrificing reconstruction quality.
T-SAEs exhibit clear semantic structure despite being trained without explicit semantic signal.
T-SAEs show improved disentanglement between high-level (semantic) and low-level (syntactic) features.
T-SAEs provide practical interpretability benefits, such as in safety monitoring and steering.
papers.abstract: Translating the internal representations and computations of models into concepts that humans can understand is a key goal of interpretability. While recent dictionary learning methods such as Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) provide a promising route to discover human-interpretable features, they suffer from a variety of problems, including a systematic failure to capture the rich conceptual information that drives linguistic understanding. Instead, they exhibit a bias towards shallow, token-specific, or noisy features, such as "the phrase 'The' at the start of sentences". In this work, we propose that this is due to a fundamental issue with how dictionary learning methods for LLMs are trained. Language itself has a rich, well-studied structure spanning syntax, semantics, and pragmatics; however, current unsupervised methods largely ignore this linguistic knowledge, leading to poor feature discovery that favors superficial patterns over meaningful concepts. We focus on a simple but important aspect of language: semantic content has long-range dependencies and tends to be smooth over a sequence, whereas syntactic information is much more local. Building on this insight, we introduce Temporal Sparse Autoencoders (T-SAEs), which incorporate a novel contrastive loss encouraging consistent activations of high-level features over adjacent tokens. This simple yet powerful modification enables SAEs to disentangle semantic from syntactic features in a self-supervised manner. Across multiple datasets and models, T-SAEs recover smoother, more coherent semantic concepts without sacrificing reconstruction quality. Strikingly, they exhibit clear semantic structure despite being trained without explicit semantic signal, offering a new pathway for unsupervised interpretability in language models.

papers.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Generalize? A Case Study of Answerability
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders capture abstract concepts like answerability in a way that generalizes across diverse datasets?
papers.core_contribution: SAE features for answerability show inconsistent out-of-domain generalization, sometimes generalizing well and sometimes poorly, indicating the need for better evaluation methods for SAE-based interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Comprehensive out-of-distribution evaluation is critical for SAE-based interpretability, as SAE features show inconsistent generalization, highlighting the need for better evaluation methods.
papers.key_findings:
Residual stream probes outperform SAE features within domains for answerability detection.
SAE features show inconsistent out-of-domain generalization, with performance varying from near-random to better than residual stream probes.
Standard SAE feature search can fail to identify generalizing features even when they exist.
Linear probes on the residual stream also exhibit high variance in generalization across datasets.
Combining multiple SAE features does not improve out-of-domain performance over the best single feature.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to Gemma 2 due to lack of high-quality SAEs for other instruction-tuned LLMs.
SAE features depend on training hyperparameters and data, affecting generalizability.
Simple SAE probe training techniques were used, which may not yield optimal results.
Feature splitting in SAEs may cause abstract concepts like answerability to be split into many separate features, complicating detection.
future_direction: Developing better evaluation methods for SAE feature generalization.
Improving SAE training methods to encourage learning of general features.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising approach in language model interpretability, offering unsupervised extraction of sparse features. For interpretability methods to succeed, they must identify abstract features across domains, and these features can often manifest differently in each context. We examine this through "answerability" - a model's ability to recognize answerable questions. We extensively evaluate SAE feature generalization across diverse, partly self-constructed answerability datasets for Gemma 2 SAEs. Our analysis reveals that residual stream probes outperform SAE features within domains, but generalization performance differs sharply. SAE features show inconsistent out-of-domain transfer, with performance varying from almost random to outperforming residual stream probes. Overall, this demonstrates the need for robust evaluation methods and quantitative approaches to predict feature generalization in SAE-based interpretability.

papers.title: A Single Direction of Truth: An Observer Model's Linear Residual Probe Exposes and Steers Contextual Hallucinations
papers.research_question: Does a transformer notice when a span of text contradicts its earlier context, and if so, is that realisation encoded along a single, linearly accessible axis that can be read out by another model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates a generator-agnostic observer model that detects contextual hallucinations via a single forward pass and a linear probe on its residual stream, isolating a single, transferable linear direction that causally steers hallucination rates.
papers.conclusion: The work provides evidence for a single, transferable, and causally effective linear direction within transformer activations corresponding to contextual hallucination, primarily processed by a sparse MLP sub-circuit, and demonstrates its utility for detection and controlled generation.
papers.key_findings:
A linear probe on the residual stream achieves high F1 scores for hallucination detection, outperforming lexical, entity, semantic, and attention-based baselines by 5–27 points.
The hallucination direction is robust across model sizes (Gemma-2 2B to 27B) and transfers across news domains with minimal performance loss.
Gradient-times-activation attribution localizes the signal to a sparse, consistent pattern of late-layer MLP activity (positive in layers 7-8, negative in layer 9 for a layer 10 probe).
Causal interventions by patching the learned direction into a generator model can steer hallucination and repetition rates bidirectionally.
Unsupervised domain adaptation by fine-tuning the observer on correct-only text from the target domain improves probe F1 scores (e.g., from 0.75 to 0.89 for Gemma-2-9B on CONTRA TALES).
papers.limitation:
Reliance on synthetically generated hallucinations for training and evaluation, which may not represent naturally occurring hallucinations.
Evaluation of steering experiments relies on a GPT-4.1 judge, which can be subject to noise, bias, and variability.
The observer paradigm requires deploying a capable transformer model, incurring computational cost compared to surface-level heuristics.
Focus on intrinsic hallucinations (contradicting source context); applicability to extrinsic hallucinations (introducing unverifiable external information) remains untested.
papers.abstract: Contextual hallucinations -- statements unsupported by given context -- remain a significant challenge in AI. We demonstrate a practical interpretability insight: a generator-agnostic observer model detects hallucinations via a single forward pass and a linear probe on its residual stream. This probe isolates a single, transferable linear direction separating hallucinated from faithful text, outperforming baselines by 5-27 points and showing robust mid-layer performance across Gemma-2 models (2B to 27B). Gradient-times-activation localises this signal to sparse, late-layer MLP activity. Critically, manipulating this direction causally steers generator hallucination rates, proving its actionability. Our results offer novel evidence of internal, low-dimensional hallucination tracking linked to specific MLP sub-circuits, exploitable for detection and mitigation. We release the 2000-example ContraTales benchmark for realistic assessment of such solutions.

papers.title: Llama Scope: Extracting Millions of Features from Llama-3.1-8B with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we scalably train Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) on large language models, and how do these SAEs perform in terms of sparsity-fidelity trade-off, interpretability, and generalization to longer contexts and fine-tuned models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Llama Scope, a suite of 256 Sparse Autoencoders trained on every layer and sublayer of Llama-3.1-8B-Base, along with modifications to Top-K SAEs and a scalable training infrastructure, providing a resource for mechanistic interpretability research.
papers.conclusion: Llama Scope provides a comprehensive set of SAEs that advance the Pareto frontier of sparsity and reconstruction fidelity, and the SAEs generalize effectively to out-of-distribution settings, facilitating future interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
TopK SAEs outperform vanilla SAEs in sparsity-fidelity trade-off.
Wider SAEs (with more features) achieve better reconstruction quality at the same sparsity level.
SAEs trained on base models generalize well to longer contexts and instruction-finetuned models.
Feature geometry analysis confirms that feature splitting enables the discovery of new features.
The firing frequency distribution of SAE features is consistent with expected sparsity constraints.
papers.limitation:
The monosemanticity evaluation focuses on top activations and may not capture behavior on low-activating samples.
The online activation generation method can lead to redundant computation when training multiple SAEs on the same position.
future_direction: Exploring SAE-based circuit analysis and fine-grained causal analysis.
Conducting automated prompt-based evaluations across a wide range of tasks.
Fine-tuning SAEs for long-context data.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful unsupervised method for extracting sparse representations from language models, yet scalable training remains a significant challenge. We introduce a suite of 256 SAEs, trained on each layer and sublayer of the Llama-3.1-8B-Base model, with 32K and 128K features. Modifications to a state-of-the-art SAE variant, Top-K SAEs, are evaluated across multiple dimensions. In particular, we assess the generalizability of SAEs trained on base models to longer contexts and fine-tuned models. Additionally, we analyze the geometry of learned SAE latents, confirming that \emph{feature splitting} enables the discovery of new features. The Llama Scope SAE checkpoints are publicly available at~\url{https://huggingface.co/fnlp/Llama-Scope}, alongside our scalable training, interpretation, and visualization tools at \url{https://github.com/OpenMOSS/Language-Model-SAEs}. These contributions aim to advance the open-source Sparse Autoencoder ecosystem and support mechanistic interpretability research by reducing the need for redundant SAE training.

papers.title: H-Neurons: On the Existence, Impact, and Origin of Hallucination-Associated Neurons in LLMs
papers.research_question: Do hallucination-associated neurons (H-Neurons) exist in LLMs, how do they influence model behavior, and when do they originate?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sparse set of hallucination-associated neurons (H-Neurons) in LLMs, demonstrates their causal link to over-compliance behaviors, and traces their origin to the pre-training phase.
papers.conclusion: Hallucinations are rooted in the model's computational architecture and training objectives, and neuron-level analysis provides insights for developing more reliable LLMs through improved detection and targeted interventions.
papers.key_findings:
A remarkably sparse subset of neurons (less than 0.1% of total) can reliably predict hallucination occurrences.
These H-Neurons are causally linked to over-compliance behaviors, including invalid premises, misleading contexts, sycophancy, and harmful instructions.
H-Neurons originate during pre-training and are not introduced by post-training alignment.
H-Neurons generalize effectively across models, domains, and hallucination types.
Interventions scaling H-Neurons activations systematically alter model compliance rates.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to knowledge-based question answering and neurons in feedforward networks.
Simple suppression or amplification of neuron activations is insufficient for effective control, balancing hallucination reduction with model helpfulness remains a challenge.
future_direction: Develop more sophisticated intervention strategies that can reliably suppress hallucinations while preserving model utility.
Extend the analysis to other model components such as attention heads.
Apply neuron-level signals for token-level hallucination detection.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently generate hallucinations -- plausible but factually incorrect outputs -- undermining their reliability. While prior work has examined hallucinations from macroscopic perspectives such as training data and objectives, the underlying neuron-level mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we conduct a systematic investigation into hallucination-associated neurons (H-Neurons) in LLMs from three perspectives: identification, behavioral impact, and origins. Regarding their identification, we demonstrate that a remarkably sparse subset of neurons (less than $0.1\%$ of total neurons) can reliably predict hallucination occurrences, with strong generalization across diverse scenarios. In terms of behavioral impact, controlled interventions reveal that these neurons are causally linked to over-compliance behaviors. Concerning their origins, we trace these neurons back to the pre-trained base models and find that these neurons remain predictive for hallucination detection, indicating they emerge during pre-training. Our findings bridge macroscopic behavioral patterns with microscopic neural mechanisms, offering insights for developing more reliable LLMs.

papers.title: Mitigating Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models with Internal Fact-based Contrastive Decoding
papers.research_question: How can object hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models be mitigated during inference by exploiting the models' own hallucinations through internal representation editing and contrastive decoding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces IFCD, a model-agnostic method that uses internal representation editing to induce and contrast hallucinatory distributions, reducing object hallucinations in LVLMs during inference without costly training.
papers.conclusion: IFCD effectively mitigates object hallucinations in LVLMs through internal representation editing and contrastive decoding, as demonstrated by experiments on multiple benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
IFCD improves accuracy on POPE by up to 9% and on MME by 8%, reducing object hallucinations.
Editing internal representations amplifies language bias and hallucinations in LVLMs.
IFCD is effective across different LVLMs like LLaVA 1.5 and InstructBLIP.
The method requires minimal training and computational resources.
Ablation studies show the importance of contrasting hallucination-induced and anti-hallucination distributions.
papers.abstract: Large Visual Language Models (LVLMs) integrate visual and linguistic modalities, exhibiting exceptional performance across various multimodal tasks. Nevertheless, LVLMs remain vulnerable to the issue of object hallucinations. Previous efforts to mitigate this issue focus on supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or incorporating external knowledge, both of which entail significant costs related to training and the acquisition of external data. To address these challenges, we propose a novel model-agnostic approach termed Internal Fact-based Contrastive Decoding (IFCD), designed to mitigate and suppress hallucinations during the inference process of LVLMs by exploiting the LVLMs' own hallucinations. IFCD is grounded in experimental observations that alterations to the LVLMs' internal representations tend to amplify hallucinations caused by language bias. By contrasting disturbed distribution, IFCD calibrates the LVLMs' output and effectively removes the hallucinatory logits from the final predictions. Experimental results validate that IFCD significantly alleviates both object-level and attribute-level hallucinations while achieving an average 9% accuracy improvement on POPE and 8% accuracy improvement on MME object hallucinations subset compared with direct decoding, respectively.

papers.title: SAE-FiRE: Enhancing Earnings Surprise Predictions Through Sparse Autoencoder Feature Selection
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to enhance earnings surprise predictions from lengthy financial documents by reducing noise and improving feature selection?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes SAE-FiRE, a framework that uses sparse autoencoders to extract and select discriminative features from LLM representations for earnings surprise prediction, demonstrating improved performance and robustness across financial datasets.
papers.conclusion: SAE-FiRE effectively suppresses noise in financial documents and improves earnings surprise prediction, offering robust performance and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-FiRE significantly outperforms baseline models like zero-shot prompting, long-document models, and hidden state probes across multiple metrics.
Tree-based feature selection methods yield better performance than ANOVA F-tests for identifying discriminative SAE features.
Intermediate transformer layers (e.g., Layer 12) provide the most predictive SAE activations compared to early or late layers.
Larger language models (e.g., Gemma2-9B) improve prediction performance due to richer representations.
SAE-FiRE enhances interpretability by identifying semantic features relevant to earnings surprises.
papers.limitation:
Relies on pretrained sparse autoencoders not optimized for financial domain adaptation.
Feature selection methods may discard weakly informative but complementary signals.
Binary classification simplifies the nuanced nature of earnings surprises.
Real-time deployment and inference efficiency are challenging due to high dimensionality.
future_direction: Extend SAE-FiRE to multimodal settings by incorporating audio features from earnings calls.
Adapt the framework to cross-lingual corporate disclosures.
Apply SAE-FiRE to other financial prediction tasks like credit risk or stock volatility modeling.
papers.abstract: Predicting earnings surprises from financial documents, such as earnings conference calls, regulatory filings, and financial news, has become increasingly important in financial economics. However, these financial documents present significant analytical challenges, typically containing over 5,000 words with substantial redundancy and industry-specific terminology that creates obstacles for language models. In this work, we propose the SAE-FiRE (Sparse Autoencoder for Financial Representation Enhancement) framework to address these limitations by extracting key information while eliminating redundancy. SAE-FiRE employs Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to decompose dense neural representations from large language models into interpretable sparse components, then applies statistical feature selection methods, including ANOVA F-tests and tree-based importance scoring, to identify the top-k most discriminative dimensions for classification. By systematically filtering out noise that might otherwise lead to overfitting, we enable more robust and generalizable predictions. Experimental results across three financial datasets demonstrate that SAE-FiRE significantly outperforms baseline approaches.

papers.title: From Flat to Hierarchical: Extracting Sparse Representations with Matching Pursuit
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can capture hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural network representations, and whether a new SAE architecture (MP-SAE) can better capture such structures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MP-SAE, a sparse autoencoder based on matching pursuit, which captures hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural representations, outperforming existing SAEs and revealing cross-modal structure in vision-language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that interpretability methods should be grounded in the phenomenology of representations, and that MP-SAE provides a step in this direction by capturing hierarchical and nonlinear structures.
papers.key_findings:
Existing SAEs struggle to capture conditionally orthogonal (hierarchical) features, while MP-SAE can capture both intra-level and inter-level structure.
MP-SAE recovers more expressive features than standard SAEs across various vision models, achieving higher reconstruction accuracy at comparable sparsity.
MP-SAE enables adaptive sparsity at inference time, allowing monotonic improvement in reconstruction error with each step, unlike fixed-sparsity SAEs.
MP-SAE learns dictionaries with higher global coherence but selects less interfering features at inference, promoting conditional orthogonality.
MP-SAE uncovers multimodal features in vision-language models that are shared across modalities, whereas standard SAEs tend to learn modality-specific features.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to hierarchical and nonlinear structures; other forms of structure (e.g., multi-dimensional features) are not addressed.
MP-SAE's inference requires multiple steps, which may be computationally more expensive than standard SAEs.
future_direction: Extending MP-SAE to capture multi-dimensional features.
Applying MP-SAE to larger-scale language models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Motivated by the hypothesis that neural network representations encode abstract, interpretable features as linearly accessible, approximately orthogonal directions, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a popular tool in interpretability. However, recent work has demonstrated phenomenology of model representations that lies outside the scope of this hypothesis, showing signatures of hierarchical, nonlinear, and multi-dimensional features. This raises the question: do SAEs represent features that possess structure at odds with their motivating hypothesis? If not, does avoiding this mismatch help identify said features and gain further insights into neural network representations? To answer these questions, we take a construction-based approach and re-contextualize the popular matching pursuits (MP) algorithm from sparse coding to design MP-SAE -- an SAE that unrolls its encoder into a sequence of residual-guided steps, allowing it to capture hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features. Comparing this architecture with existing SAEs on a mixture of synthetic and natural data settings, we show: (i) hierarchical concepts induce conditionally orthogonal features, which existing SAEs are unable to faithfully capture, and (ii) the nonlinear encoding step of MP-SAE recovers highly meaningful features, helping us unravel shared structure in the seemingly dichotomous representation spaces of different modalities in a vision-language model, hence demonstrating the assumption that useful features are solely linearly accessible is insufficient. We also show that the sequential encoder principle of MP-SAE affords an additional benefit of adaptive sparsity at inference time, which may be of independent interest. Overall, we argue our results provide credence to the idea that interpretability should begin with the phenomenology of representations, with methods emerging from assumptions that fit it.

papers.title: In-Context Sharpness as Alerts: An Inner Representation Perspective for Hallucination Mitigation
papers.research_question: Why do large language models (LLMs) hallucinate and produce factual errors, and can this be understood and mitigated by analyzing their inner representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that correct model generations have sharper context activations (lower entropy) in hidden states, and introduces Activation Decoding, a constrained decoding method that uses this entropy metric to adjust token probabilities and mitigate hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies in-context sharpness as a critical signal for hallucination and proposes Activation Decoding, an effective method for enhancing the factuality of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Correct generations tend to have sharper context activations in the hidden states of in-context tokens compared to incorrect ones.
An entropy-based metric quantifying this 'in-context sharpness' can differentiate between correct and incorrect answers with high AUROC (up to 0.76).
Activation Decoding, which incorporates the entropy metric into the decoding process, consistently improves factuality across various knowledge-seeking and truthfulness benchmarks and model sizes.
The method is inference-efficient as entropy values for prompt tokens can be precomputed, adding minimal latency.
Activation Decoding can be combined with other decoding methods (e.g., Dola) for further performance gains, suggesting complementary hallucination patterns.
papers.limitation:
The method cannot address errors requiring external knowledge, such as outdated facts or errors in the training data.
Representation-based methods have an inherent performance ceiling and may correct some errors while unintentionally generating new ones.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently hallucinate and produce factual errors, yet our understanding of why they make these errors remains limited. In this study, we delve into the underlying mechanisms of LLM hallucinations from the perspective of inner representations, and discover a salient pattern associated with hallucinations: correct generations tend to have sharper context activations in the hidden states of the in-context tokens, compared to the incorrect ones. Leveraging this insight, we propose an entropy-based metric to quantify the ``sharpness'' among the in-context hidden states and incorporate it into the decoding process to formulate a constrained decoding approach. Experiments on various knowledge-seeking and hallucination benchmarks demonstrate our approach's consistent effectiveness, for example, achieving up to an 8.6 point improvement on TruthfulQA. We believe this study can improve our understanding of hallucinations and serve as a practical solution for hallucination mitigation.

papers.title: Evaluating Open-Source Sparse Autoencoders on Disentangling Factual Knowledge in GPT-2 Small
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoder (SAE) feature spaces are useful for causal interpretability analysis, specifically for disentangling related factual knowledge (country and continent of cities) in language models.
papers.core_contribution: Current open-source sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for GPT-2 small struggle to provide a feature space that better disentangles factual knowledge than the baseline of neurons, and none approach the performance of the supervised DAS skyline.
papers.conclusion: Only one of the evaluated SAEs reached the neuron baseline and none reached the DAS skyline, indicating current SAEs are not superior to neurons for this causal disentanglement task, but the evaluation is a useful step for assessing SAEs in interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Using representations reconstructed by SAEs degrades the model's knowledge of cities.
The end-to-end SAEs degrade knowledge less relative to their reconstruction loss, but this is weak evidence.
There is a significant gap between the neuron baseline and the DAS skyline, showing neurons can be improved upon.
Current SAEs for GPT-2 small generally perform below the neuron baseline, with only the top-k Open AI SAE matching it.
The top-k SAE (Open AI SAE) is the most performant among the evaluated SAEs.
papers.limitation: The evaluation is limited to GPT-2 small and a specific dataset (cities, countries, continents). Future work should scale to larger models and more attributes.
future_direction: Scale experiments to models with available SAEs including gemma, Mistral, Llama, and Pythia.
Use more attributes from the RA VEL dataset, such as language, gender, etc., for larger models with more knowledge.
papers.abstract: A popular new method in mechanistic interpretability is to train high-dimensional sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on neuron activations and use SAE features as the atomic units of analysis. However, the body of evidence on whether SAE feature spaces are useful for causal analysis is underdeveloped. In this work, we use the RAVEL benchmark to evaluate whether SAEs trained on hidden representations of GPT-2 small have sets of features that separately mediate knowledge of which country a city is in and which continent it is in. We evaluate four open-source SAEs for GPT-2 small against each other, with neurons serving as a baseline, and linear features learned via distributed alignment search (DAS) serving as a skyline. For each, we learn a binary mask to select features that will be patched to change the country of a city without changing the continent, or vice versa. Our results show that SAEs struggle to reach the neuron baseline, and none come close to the DAS skyline. We release code here: https://github.com/MaheepChaudhary/SAE-Ravel

papers.title: Mechanistic Understanding and Mitigation of Language Model Non-Factual Hallucinations
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanistic causes of non-factual hallucinations in language models, and how can they be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies two mechanistic causes of non-factual hallucinations in LMs—knowledge enrichment failures in lower MLPs and answer extraction failures in upper attention heads—and proposes a mitigation method based on restoring the internal fact recall pipeline.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that abnormal operation of lower MLPs and upper attention heads leads to distinct hallucination mechanisms, and introduces an effective mitigation method based on mechanistic insights.
papers.key_findings:
Hallucinations are caused by two distinct mechanisms: knowledge enrichment failures in lower layer MLPs and answer extraction failures in upper layer attention heads.
These mechanisms have different external manifestations, such as subject-object association strengths and robustness to input perturbations.
The proposed MHM method effectively mitigates hallucinations by targeting both MLP and attention components during fine-tuning.
MHM outperforms baselines like SFT, ICL, MEND, and DoLa on open-domain QA datasets.
The findings are consistent across multiple LMs including Llama-2, Pythia, and GPT-J.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on logit lens for interpreting intermediate layers, which only approximates encoded information.
Focus on simple input sequences may not capture real-world LM behavior with complex contexts.
future_direction: Use more sophisticated methods like Tuned Lens to probe layer information.
Apply mechanistic interpretability to more complex and naturalistic contexts.
papers.abstract: State-of-the-art language models (LMs) sometimes generate non-factual hallucinations that misalign with world knowledge. To explore the mechanistic causes of these hallucinations, we create diagnostic datasets with subject-relation queries and adapt interpretability methods to trace hallucinations through internal model representations. We discover two general and distinct mechanistic causes of hallucinations shared across LMs (Llama-2, Pythia, GPT-J): 1) knowledge enrichment hallucinations: insufficient subject attribute knowledge in lower layer MLPs, and 2) answer extraction hallucinations: failure to select the correct object attribute in upper layer attention heads. We also found these two internal mechanistic causes of hallucinations are reflected in external manifestations. Based on insights from our mechanistic analysis, we propose a novel hallucination mitigation method through targeted restoration of the LM's internal fact recall pipeline, demonstrating superior performance compared to baselines.

papers.title: Enhancing Neural Network Interpretability with Feature-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the feature learning of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to better align with input features, thereby enhancing their usefulness for neural network interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Mutual Feature Regularization (MFR), a regularization technique that trains multiple Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) in parallel with weight reinitialization and an auxiliary penalty to encourage learning similar features, leading to better alignment with input features and improved SAE performance.
papers.conclusion: MFR encourages SAEs to learn more features of the input, thereby increasing their usefulness for neural network interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
MFR increases the correlation between feature similarity across SAEs and similarity with input features, as demonstrated on synthetic data.
On synthetic data, SAEs trained with MFR recover more of the known input features compared to baseline SAEs.
MFR improves reconstruction loss and loss recovered when training SAEs on GPT-2 Small MLP layer activations, with up to a 21.21% reduction in reconstruction loss.
MFR also improves reconstruction loss on EEG denoising tasks, though the benefits are smaller than for neural network activations.
The method involves conditionally reinitializing SAE weights based on inactive feature detection and adding an auxiliary penalty to encourage feature similarity across SAEs.
papers.limitation: MFR increases computational cost as it requires training multiple SAEs in parallel, which may become unmanageable for very large models.
future_direction: Investigate efficient mutual learning-based approaches for SAEs that can benefit from the positive relationship between feature similarity across SAEs and feature similarity with input features without requiring more compute.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promise in improving the interpretability of neural network activations, but can learn features that are not features of the input, limiting their effectiveness. We propose \textsc{Mutual Feature Regularization} \textbf{(MFR)}, a regularization technique for improving feature learning by encouraging SAEs trained in parallel to learn similar features. We motivate \textsc{MFR} by showing that features learned by multiple SAEs are more likely to correlate with features of the input. By training on synthetic data with known features of the input, we show that \textsc{MFR} can help SAEs learn those features, as we can directly compare the features learned by the SAE with the input features for the synthetic data. We then scale \textsc{MFR} to SAEs that are trained to denoise electroencephalography (EEG) data and SAEs that are trained to reconstruct GPT-2 Small activations. We show that \textsc{MFR} can improve the reconstruction loss of SAEs by up to 21.21\% on GPT-2 Small, and 6.67\% on EEG data. Our results suggest that the similarity between features learned by different SAEs can be leveraged to improve SAE training, thereby enhancing performance and the usefulness of SAEs for model interpretability.

papers.title: Cross-Layer Attention Probing for Fine-Grained Hallucination Detection
papers.research_question: How can we improve hallucination detection in LLMs by probing activations across the entire residual stream?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Cross-Layer Attention Probing (CLAP), a novel probing technique that uses attention over the residual stream to improve hallucination detection in LLMs, enabling fine-grained detection and integration with mitigation strategies.
papers.conclusion: CLAP is an effective method for detecting and mitigating hallucinations in LLMs by leveraging cross-layer attention over the residual stream, outperforming existing approaches and generalizing well out-of-distribution.
papers.key_findings:
CLAP improves hallucination detection over uncertainty baselines and single-layer probes on multiple LLMs and tasks.
CLAP enables fine-grained detection of hallucinations among sampled responses to the same prompt.
Combining CLAP with mitigation strategies like DoLa reduces hallucination rates while minimizing negative impacts on non-hallucinated responses.
CLAP generalizes better out-of-distribution compared to layer-specific probes and semantic entropy probes.
Ablation studies show that cross-layer attention is crucial for CLAP's performance and generalizability.
papers.limitation:
Focused on small LLMs (2B-8B parameters), leaving scaling to larger LLMs for future work.
The role of each layer within CLAP is not investigated and left for future work.
future_direction: Scaling CLAP to larger LLMs
Investigating the role of each layer within CLAP
papers.abstract: With the large-scale adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) in various applications, there is a growing reliability concern due to their tendency to generate inaccurate text, i.e. hallucinations. In this work, we propose Cross-Layer Attention Probing (CLAP), a novel activation probing technique for hallucination detection, which processes the LLM activations across the entire residual stream as a joint sequence. Our empirical evaluations using five LLMs and three tasks show that CLAP improves hallucination detection compared to baselines on both greedy decoded responses as well as responses sampled at higher temperatures, thus enabling fine-grained detection, i.e. the ability to disambiguate hallucinations and non-hallucinations among different sampled responses to a given prompt. This allows us to propose a detect-then-mitigate strategy using CLAP to reduce hallucinations and improve LLM reliability compared to direct mitigation approaches. Finally, we show that CLAP maintains high reliability even when applied out-of-distribution.

papers.title: On Epistemic Uncertainty of Visual Tokens for Object Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How does the epistemic uncertainty of visual tokens from the vision encoder contribute to object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), and can mitigating this uncertainty reduce hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that visual tokens with high epistemic uncertainty are a key factor in object hallucination in LVLMs, and proposes a training-free method to mitigate hallucinations by identifying these uncertain tokens via adversarial perturbations and masking them in the self-attention layers of the vision encoder.
papers.conclusion: Uncertain visual tokens from the vision encoder are a key contributor to object hallucination in LVLMs, and the proposed training-free masking method effectively mitigates hallucinations by suppressing these tokens, offering a complementary approach to existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Visual tokens with high epistemic uncertainty, as estimated by representation deviation under adversarial perturbations, are strongly positively correlated with object hallucination in LVLMs.
The norm of representation deviation under small adversarial perturbations efficiently approximates an upper bound of epistemic uncertainty for visual tokens, particularly in early vision encoder layers.
Masking uncertain visual tokens in the self-attention process of intermediate vision encoder layers significantly reduces object hallucination across multiple LVLM architectures and benchmarks.
The proposed method is orthogonal and compatible with existing language-model-focused hallucination mitigation techniques, enabling synergistic performance gains.
The method reduces the average uncertainty of visual tokens, and this reduction correlates with improved hallucination metrics.
papers.limitation:
The method requires additional computational overhead for generating adversarial perturbations to identify uncertain tokens.
The threshold parameter for binarizing the uncertainty mask needs to be tuned for different models and decoding strategies.
The method may not address all types of hallucinations, such as those arising from the language model itself or from complex reasoning errors.
future_direction: Extending the uncertainty estimation and masking approach to other modalities and tasks beyond object hallucination.
Improving the efficiency of the uncertainty estimation process to reduce computational overhead.
Exploring the integration of the proposed vision-encoder-focused method with more advanced language-model-based mitigation techniques.
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs), which integrate a vision encoder (VE) with a large language model, have achieved remarkable success across various tasks. However, there are still crucial challenges in LVLMs such as object hallucination, generating descriptions of objects that are not in the input image. Here, we argue that uncertain visual tokens within the VE is a key factor that contributes to object hallucination. Our statistical analysis found that there are positive correlations between visual tokens with high epistemic uncertainty and the occurrence of hallucinations. Furthermore, we show theoretically and empirically that visual tokens in early VE layers that exhibit large representation deviations under small adversarial perturbations indicate high epistemic uncertainty. Based on these findings, we propose a simple yet effective strategy to mitigate object hallucination by modifying the VE only. Our method comprises a proxy method with adversarial perturbations for identifying uncertain visual tokens efficiently and a method to mask these uncertain visual tokens during the self-attention process in the middle layers of the VE, suppressing their influence on visual encoding and thus alleviating hallucinations. Extensive experiments show that our method significantly reduces object hallucinations in LVLMs and can synergistically work with other prior arts.

papers.title: Beyond Activation Patterns: A Weight-Based Out-of-Context Explanation of Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we interpret Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features from a weight-based, out-of-context perspective to understand their computational roles, beyond activation patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a weight-based, out-of-context interpretation framework for SAE features that reveals their computational roles in output prediction and attention mechanisms, complementing activation-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Weight-based, out-of-context analysis provides the missing half of SAE feature interpretability, revealing computational roles and depth-dependent functional specialization that activation patterns alone cannot capture.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 1/4 of SAE features directly predict output tokens when analyzed through their decoder-unembedding interactions.
Semantic features exhibit a U-shaped distribution across depth in Gemma models (high in early and late layers) and a monotonic distribution in Llama models, revealing architectural differences in functional specialization.
Features actively participate in attention mechanisms, with pre- and post-softmax analysis showing depth-dependent structure and distinct profiles for semantic vs. non-semantic populations.
Weight-based analysis uncovers that early-layer features in Llama specialize for input token recognition (encoder-embedding alignment) while late-layer features specialize for output prediction (decoder-unembedding alignment).
The out-of-context framework provides a complementary, causal perspective on feature function that activation-based methods miss.
papers.limitation:
The out-of-context framework is strict and simulates attention competition across the entire SAE dictionary, which may not reflect the contextual sparsity of actual forward passes and could underestimate feature importance.
The analysis focuses on intra-layer attention (features in layer L interacting with QK circuits in layer L+1) and may miss features specialized for longer-range, inter-layer interactions.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful technique for decomposing language model representations into interpretable features. Current interpretation methods infer feature semantics from activation patterns, but overlook that features are trained to reconstruct activations that serve computational roles in the forward pass. We introduce a novel weight-based interpretation framework that measures functional effects through direct weight interactions, requiring no activation data. Through three experiments on Gemma-2 and Llama-3.1 models, we demonstrate that (1) 1/4 of features directly predict output tokens, (2) features actively participate in attention mechanisms with depth-dependent structure, and (3) semantic and non-semantic feature populations exhibit distinct distribution profiles in attention circuits. Our analysis provides the missing out-of-context half of SAE feature interpretability.

papers.title: Interpreting Large Text-to-Image Diffusion Models with Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse dictionary learning methods (Sparse Autoencoders and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations) be scaled and applied to interpret and control large text-to-image diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: This work successfully scales Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA) to a large text-to-image diffusion model (FLUX.1), demonstrating they can decompose residual stream activations into interpretable features and enable targeted steering of image generation.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Autoencoders and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations are effective methods for interpreting and steering large text-to-image diffusion models, with SAE features being particularly suitable for manipulating concrete semantic concepts in generated images.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs accurately reconstruct residual stream embeddings and outperform MLP neurons on automated interpretability metrics.
ITDA achieves comparable interpretability to SAEs but tends to encode more abstract visual attributes (colors, textures) while SAE features capture more concrete objects.
Steering image generation via SAE feature activation addition is effective but constrained, requiring the initial prompt to be semantically related to the steered feature.
The residual stream activations in FLUX.1 are highly anisotropic, necessitating PCA whitening for effective SAE training to avoid a high proportion of dead features.
ITDA generally achieves superior reconstruction performance compared to SAEs at similar dictionary sizes.
papers.limitation:
Automated interpretability (autointerp) metrics do not distinguish between abstract visual properties and manipulable semantic concepts, a qualitative difference observed between ITDA and SAE features.
Steering with SAE features is constrained and only effective when the initial image prompt is semantically related to the feature being added.
The autointerp pipeline may have biases, such as picking up on simple image characteristics like color rather than the intended semantic feature.
future_direction: Applying SAEs to vision tasks like classification, segmentation, and depth estimation (sparse probing).
Adapting the SAE encoder architecture to incorporate spatial inductive bias (e.g., convolutional layers) for image data.
Improving steering techniques, potentially by making the process more similar to finetuning or otherwise more aware of steering effects.
Investigating shared features between the text and image streams of the multimodal DiT architecture.
Comparing the two FLUX.1 variants (Dev and Schnell) using methods like crosscoders to find corresponding or unique features.
Investigating biases specific to the automated interpretability pipeline.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders are a promising new approach for decomposing language model activations for interpretation and control. They have been applied successfully to vision transformer image encoders and to small-scale diffusion models. Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA) is a recently proposed variant of dictionary learning that takes the dictionary to be a set of data points from the activation distribution and reconstructs them with gradient pursuit. We apply Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and ITDA to a large text-to-image diffusion model, Flux 1, and consider the interpretability of embeddings of both by introducing a visual automated interpretation pipeline. We find that SAEs accurately reconstruct residual stream embeddings and beat MLP neurons on interpretability. We are able to use SAE features to steer image generation through activation addition. We find that ITDA has comparable interpretability to SAEs.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: Hallucination Detection in LLMs Using Spectral Features of Attention Maps
papers.research_question: How can spectral features of attention maps, interpreted as graph structures, be used to detect hallucinations in Large Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes LapEigvals, a method that uses top-k eigenvalues of the Laplacian of attention maps as features for a hallucination detection probe, achieving state-of-the-art performance among attention-based methods.
papers.conclusion: LapEigvals is a robust and effective method for hallucination detection using spectral features of attention maps, achieving state-of-the-art performance and generalizing well across models and datasets.
papers.key_findings:
LapEigvals achieves state-of-the-art hallucination detection performance among attention-based methods across multiple LLMs and datasets.
Using features from all layers of the LLM yields better performance than using a single layer.
Higher sampling temperatures during answer generation improve hallucination detection performance.
LapEigvals generalizes across different QA datasets, though performance drops on TruthfulQA and GSM8K due to dataset size and domain differences.
LapEigvals is robust to variations in the prompt used for answer generation.
papers.limitation: The method generalizes poorly on TruthfulQA due to its limited size and class imbalance, and on GSM8K due to its distinct domain.
future_direction: Further exploration of the relationship between sampling temperature and hallucination detection.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance across various tasks but remain prone to hallucinations. Detecting hallucinations is essential for safety-critical applications, and recent methods leverage attention map properties to this end, though their effectiveness remains limited. In this work, we investigate the spectral features of attention maps by interpreting them as adjacency matrices of graph structures. We propose the $\text{LapEigvals}$ method, which utilises the top-$k$ eigenvalues of the Laplacian matrix derived from the attention maps as an input to hallucination detection probes. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art hallucination detection performance among attention-based methods. Extensive ablation studies further highlight the robustness and generalisation of $\text{LapEigvals}$, paving the way for future advancements in the hallucination detection domain.

papers.title: SynthSAEBench: Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders on Scalable Realistic Synthetic Data
papers.research_question: How can we create a scalable synthetic benchmark with ground-truth features to evaluate and diagnose Sparse Autoencoder architectures?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SynthSAEBench, a toolkit and benchmark for generating large-scale synthetic data with realistic feature characteristics (correlation, hierarchy, superposition) to evaluate and diagnose Sparse Autoencoder architectures.
papers.conclusion: SynthSAEBench complements LLM benchmarks by providing ground-truth features and controlled ablations, enabling precise diagnosis of SAE failure modes and validation of architectural improvements before scaling to LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Reproduces LLM SAE phenomena: Matryoshka SAEs overperform on probing despite poor reconstruction; MP-SAEs overperform on reconstruction but poor probing; poor SAE probing relative to supervised probes; precision-recall trade-off mediated by L0.
Identifies a new failure mode: MP-SAEs exploit superposition noise to improve reconstruction without learning ground-truth features, suggesting expressive encoders can overfit.
No SAE architecture achieves perfect performance on SynthSAEBench-16k, highlighting a target for architectural improvement.
papers.limitation: The synthetic model cannot capture all aspects of real neural network representations.
future_direction: Extend the framework to Minkowski representations and feature manifolds.
Understand the performance gap between JumpReLU and BatchTopK SAEs.
papers.abstract: Improving Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) requires benchmarks that can precisely validate architectural innovations. However, current SAE benchmarks on LLMs are often too noisy to differentiate architectural improvements, and current synthetic data experiments are too small-scale and unrealistic to provide meaningful comparisons. We introduce SynthSAEBench, a toolkit for generating large-scale synthetic data with realistic feature characteristics including correlation, hierarchy, and superposition, and a standardized benchmark model, SynthSAEBench-16k, enabling direct comparison of SAE architectures. Our benchmark reproduces several previously observed LLM SAE phenomena, including the disconnect between reconstruction and latent quality metrics, poor SAE probing results, and a precision-recall trade-off mediated by L0. We further use our benchmark to identify a new failure mode: Matching Pursuit SAEs exploit superposition noise to improve reconstruction without learning ground-truth features, suggesting that more expressive encoders can easily overfit. SynthSAEBench complements LLM benchmarks by providing ground-truth features and controlled ablations, enabling researchers to precisely diagnose SAE failure modes and validate architectural improvements before scaling to LLMs.

papers.title: Interpreting and Steering LLMs with Mutual Information-based Explanations on Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How to better explain sparse autoencoder features in LLMs to capture semantic meaning and use these explanations to steer LLM behaviors, particularly for defending against jailbreak attacks.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a mutual information-based explanation method for sparse autoencoder features that mitigates frequency bias and enables effective steering of LLM behaviors, particularly for enhancing safety against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that discourse-level explanations from sparse autoencoders are crucial for understanding and steering LLM behaviors, particularly for safety applications.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretical analysis reveals frequency bias in sparse autoencoder features between discourse topics and linguistic patterns.
The proposed mutual information-based method generates more discourse-level explanations compared to baseline methods like TopAct and N2G.
The discourse-level explanations are effective in steering LLM behaviors to defend against jailbreak attacks.
Experiments show a higher successful explained rate for features with the proposed method.
Steering strategies such as amplification and calibration can enhance LLM safety without additional model training.
papers.limitation: The approach relies on existing sparse autoencoders without modifying their architectures or training to mitigate frequency bias.
future_direction: Designing improved architectures or training objectives for sparse autoencoders to inherently mitigate frequency bias.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at handling human queries, but they can occasionally generate flawed or unexpected responses. Understanding their internal states is crucial for understanding their successes, diagnosing their failures, and refining their capabilities. Although sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promise for interpreting LLM internal representations, limited research has explored how to better explain SAE features, i.e., understanding the semantic meaning of features learned by SAE. Our theoretical analysis reveals that existing explanation methods suffer from the frequency bias issue, where they emphasize linguistic patterns over semantic concepts, while the latter is more critical to steer LLM behaviors. To address this, we propose using a fixed vocabulary set for feature interpretations and designing a mutual information-based objective, aiming to better capture the semantic meaning behind these features. We further propose two runtime steering strategies that adjust the learned feature activations based on their corresponding explanations. Empirical results show that, compared to baselines, our method provides more discourse-level explanations and effectively steers LLM behaviors to defend against jailbreak attacks. These findings highlight the value of explanations for steering LLM behaviors in downstream applications. We will release our code and data once accepted.

papers.title: LRP4RAG: Detecting Hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Layer-wise Relevance Propagation
papers.research_question: How can we detect hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) by analyzing the relevance between the retrieved context and the model's output?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes LRP4RAG, a novel hallucination detection method for RAG that uses Layer-wise Relevance Propagation to analyze context-answer relevance, outperforming existing baselines.
papers.conclusion: LRP4RAG is an effective method for detecting hallucinations in RAG and provides new insights into the causes and characteristics of hallucinations from a relevance-based perspective.
papers.key_findings:
LRP4RAG outperforms 10 state-of-the-art baselines on two benchmarks (RAGTruth and Dolly-15k) across six metrics.
LRP4RAG improves the most recent baseline SEP by 4.1% and 5.1% in accuracy.
It is the first work to apply additive interpretability to hallucination detection in RAG.
Analysis reveals that long context and mismatch between model's explicit words and internal thoughts are causes of hallucinations in RAG.
papers.limitation: LRP4RAGLLM requires significantly greater computational resources and longer processing times compared to classifier-based variants.
future_direction: Improving the efficiency of LRP4RAG, especially the LRP backward stage.
Extending LRP4RAG to other NLP tasks such as summarization and machine translation.
Exploring other interpretability methods beyond LRP for hallucination detection.
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become a primary technique for mitigating hallucinations in large language models (LLMs). However, incomplete knowledge extraction and insufficient understanding can still mislead LLMs to produce irrelevant or even contradictory responses, which means hallucinations persist in RAG. In this paper, we propose LRP4RAG, a method based on the Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) algorithm for detecting hallucinations in RAG. Specifically, we first utilize LRP to compute the relevance between the input and output of the RAG generator. We then apply further extraction and resampling to the relevance matrix. The processed relevance data are input into multiple classifiers to determine whether the output contains hallucinations. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time that LRP has been used for detecting RAG hallucinations, and extensive experiments demonstrate that LRP4RAG outperforms existing baselines.

papers.title: On Early Detection of Hallucinations in Factual Question Answering
papers.research_question: Whether model artifacts (like token attributions, softmax probabilities, attention scores, and activations) can provide signals for detecting hallucinations in factual question answering.
papers.core_contribution: Model artifacts (softmax probabilities, attention scores, activations, and token attributions) can be used to detect hallucinations in factual question answering, and hallucinations can be detected even before they occur (at the first generation token).
papers.conclusion: Attaching classifiers based on model artifacts can flag potentially incorrect information before it reaches end-users, providing an effective method for hallucination detection.
papers.key_findings:
